title: Dillon Thieneman says coming to Chicago was meant to be | Press Conference
text: What have the last 24 hours been like for you? Obviously waking up yesterday and not knowing where you're going to be spending the next whatever decade of your life and now all of a sudden you're here. >> Yeah. Um it's been a great experience. Like a lot of moving around like being in Pittsburgh and going to different events, the red carpet then the green room and coming out here. But um it's been incredible. I'm happy to be here. >> Were you able to get any sleep last night or like what was it? >> A little bit. I was thinking about it a lot but I was able to sleep a little bit. What were your impressions just walking through the building, especially that players entrance and just what's kind of going through your mind as you see the numbers and names of the people played in for this team? >> Yeah. Uh I know this team has a lot of history. Um and it's been awesome to to kind of see that displayed as you walk through the building and um I'm just happy to get in and get to work. >> How much did you know about that growing up not too far away from here? >> Um I know a little bit. Um, I was really young when we were as a family a Bears team, but um, I'm excited to learn more. Were >> you a Colts guy growing up? Obviously. >> Yeah, when we moved down to Indianapolis, we were Colts, but still had the Bears in there somewhere. >> Last night you said that you connected with the Bears at the combine in a in an interview. What exact expand on that? What what exactly about the interview was positive? >> Yeah, I mean, uh, overall I felt like there was a lot of positive energy going around. Um, it felt easy. It was great to talk to the team. Like they had a lot of guys in there. Um and then me sitting in like the one chair that's kind of standing out, but um they're just asking some background questions, talking through some film. Then they have me get on the whiteboard a little bit. >> You said yesterday that you were a little almost like surprised like I know you had the meeting with them at the combine and then not a whole ton of connection with them in between then and when you were drafted. Did you think you were go was there somewhere on the board that you had circled that you thought you'd be going before you wind up at 25 here? Um overall like we had ideas so wherever I might go but um in the moment I kind of just stayed calm and and prayed I hope I got to the right spot and I think this was the right spot. So I mean through that process like we talked at the combine um they showed their interest. I heard a lot from them like through other people and then it all worked out in the end. when you were making a decision to transfer from Purdue to Oregon, what were you envisioning for that that next year? And and what do you in retrospect, what do you think you accomplished by by making that move? >> Um, I mean, going into that that year at Oregon, um, I had the goal set that I want to go one year and go. Um, so going through that and I wanted to to put everything I could into that knowing that, um, if I did decide to stay, it was the right decision. If I decided to leave, I put everything in. So, I made the right choice going to Oregon. Um, and what was the the second part of your question? >> What do you think you accomplished when you look back on your year in Oregon? >> Uh, I think I accomplished a lot. I know we came up short, um, but I made some great connections with those coaches and those teammates that I'll probably have rest of my life. >> It sound It sounded like they coached you very hard at Oregon. Even uh even some of the talks they had with you kind of recruiting you to transfer there, they were pretty tough on you. um what made you receptive to that and how do you think that made you better? >> Um in the recruiting process like out of out of high school and transferring in college um it's more like the player picks. So a lot of people are I guess like sugar coating it or trying to trying to talk you up and uh talking with H talking with Lanning like they didn't sugarcoat anything. They told me exactly like we think you're a good player. This is what you need to work on. This is how we can get you better. This is how we develop guys in the past. Um, and to see those examples and see how they had a plan for me, um, made a very easy decision. >> Dylan, what do you remember, uh, from learning under Jake Gilbert? He was saying that, uh, even as in youth football, you were out running guys in high school. >> Um, Coach Gilbert always liked talking about TNTs, that tank, no talents. So, always it's a effort and attitude. So, I mean, effort, just running the ball is is one thing that everyone can do, doesn't matter what your talent level is. So he also said that your dad uh used to tell you um skate to where the puck is going to be. You remember that and what that means your interpretation? >> Um I don't remember it as much. My idea is that it's probably like more of a feel for the game. So how's how's the how's the pocket moving? What are they trying to attack? Um and just be aggressive to the point of attack. >> You talked about the the studies you put into your role and other roles on the defense. Where does your passion for football come from? What makes you put in the work that you do for this game? >> It starts with that that little kid, the four-year-old me looking up that TV, being like, "Hey, it's going to be me out there." Um, but then it goes into to seeing my family and my brothers do it. Um, see my parents, how they work in their businesses. And, uh, really watching my brothers out there on the field, wanting to be out there with them. Um, and then I'm I'm someone I think like if I if I really love something, I'm going to put all my energy, all my work into it. Are are you able to use that kind of perspective of understanding and appreciating this moment today and last night? >> Yes. Yeah. I know this is once a lifetime moment, so you just got to you got to take it all in and u just enjoy it. >> What do you remember your football acumen in playing that rover role at Oregon? How did that, I guess, expand your football IQ and prepare you to for what you're about to do in the NFL and just the vers like changing the versatility or like strengthening the versatility of your game? >> Yeah. Um that position really allows you to play fast. you you uh can be aggressive in the run game because a lot of times um just the distance I'm off from the line of scrimmage, I'm I'm the extra unblocked defender. Um and then the pass game that playing that rover roll, you're kind of that middle of the field. So you're what what the offense most likely like like once the target a lot of times. So um that just allowed me a lot more opportunities to get around the ball, get more experience and uh just think about what the offense is trying what they're showing me in their formations and or situations and what they're trying to attack. polls up last night that like the way you play is what it takes the oxygen out of an offense. Um, is there a play that you remember from college that like you felt that energy? You felt that same thing like the play it just like completely decimated what they were doing? >> Um, I mean, one of them is the the Penn State game just at the end of the game. Um just to I mean it's a white out game, college game day and the stadium's going super loud, double overtime and to to get the pick and then everything just goes silent and I could hear my all the Oregon fans and and my family kind of yelling up in the stands. So that one was awesome. >> Dylan, how do you calculate when to take risk as a defender and when to just stay more sound and responsibility? >> Um I think that just comes more with experience. So, experience watching the game, experience playing uh going against certain teams, certain offenses, and uh playing in different defensive schemes and the and trusting your guys around you. Um so, I can't tell you like this, I do that. Another situation, you do this. It's more of just a feel for >> Dude, Dylan, going back to going back to your family, how do you think being the youngest of three brothers kind of shaped you athletically, maybe as a competitor? It >> definitely helped me. like they were they were a good amount of years older than me. So to see what they're doing, they were kind of just teaching it, applying it to me. So I got it at a much younger age than other people would have gotten it or that they got at their age. Um so I feel like that just spread up my u development and allowed me to >> always at games, always at the gym, just always >> be what do you what do you remember about facing Coulson when you were at Purdue? Um, I know that they won and >> they won a lot of games. >> Yes, they won a lot of games. Um, but no, he's an extremely talented player. I didn't get to to match up with him specifically in that game because of our defensive scheme, but I know he's a great player. >> And JJ McCarthy, too. He's somebody who's now in your division and depending on what happens there may start for them. What do you do you have any memory of of him? Uh, not a whole lot, but I I can't wait to to face him again. >> Having been in the Pacific Northwest, how much did you watch Kobe Bryant and now getting a chance to play alongside him and learn from him here with the Bears? >> Uh, I wasn't able to watch a whole lot of him, but I'm I'm very excited to to get the chance to to learn from him and and to work with him. >> Did you have a favorite player growing up or somebody you tried to emulate your game after? Uh, I really like I liked watching or going back and watching once I was older. Um, like Troy Palmer, Ed Reed. Um, and then currently I like I watch various players around the league. So, I like to kind of like take a little bit um, see where I can learn something and then kind of make it my own. >> Have you heard from any of your new teammates over the last 24 hours? >> Yeah, Colston. Coloulston text me I think right away. Um, I'm sure someone else has texted me. I haven't been able to go through them all. What Colston tell you? >> He was just like, "Yo, glad to have you on the team. Can't wait to get to work. Let me know if you need anything." >> What's been your interaction so far with either Ben or or Dennis Allen? >> Yeah, I just had a few meetings with them. It was great meeting just sitting down talking about um how they see my role in the team and and what they think we can do.

title: Ryan Poles on Dillon Thieneman: 'Everything we're looking for' | Press Conference
text: Ryan, when did the man first come on your radar and maybe some of your first impressions of of watching him? >> Yeah. So, when we do our meetings, we go um we take the average of like the high grades uh from the fall and we work, you know, from the top down. And when we started the safety position, uh there's a couple good ones that we liked. Dylan's tape popped out like just the sense of urgency that it plays with, the speed. um we talk about taking the air, you know, out of the defense or out of the offense. His ability to close on the football both in the run and the pass um stood out really really quick. And as we watched it, the comments you could hear, I mean, this guy is obsessed with football, plays fast, he's extremely smart, u great leader, um violent in the way that he plays the game, everything that we're looking for. Then on top of that, you have some versatility. Um if he has to, he can go over and play a little bit of nickel. Um he can play free, he can play strong. So, uh, really good fit for what we're trying to do. >> How do you describe the aggressiveness in his play style? >> Oh, it's the aggressiveness. I mean, it flies up the tape. He's a violent football player. He strikes. Uh, there's a knock back element to his tackling. And, um, and again, just the speed. There's like speed and there's like violent speed in terms of just the explosion off the spot. Um, and that's what he brings and it's it's pretty easy tape to watch. Yeah. >> All right. What went into the weighing hit Dylan's strengths versus some pretty good candidates that were still there at defensive tackle, defensive end? >> Yeah. Um on our board again, you know, we're talking about the board talking to you. Um he was standing out. He was elevated on the board um at a spot. So, we kind of work lateral and see who else is up there. Um and he was the number one in our priority list. Um, we take the board before obviously all this kicks off when we sequence it and he was the top sequence guy on our on our on our board. >> Were there any anxious moments as he kind of had the board going? He was clearly your guy like J said the board was wide open. Was it getting anxious as you get closer and closer? Yeah, it it was um I think I talked about our simulator uses some mock um hundreds of mocks uh to kind of hone in and give us different challenges as we're picking to go through and simulate the draft. Um it was 50/50 with him oftent times. So we weren't sure if he was going to make it. I think there was a lot I think it was 18 seemed to be the spot that everyone said he was going to. We knew that if he got past that there's a good chance. Um, again, we in our sequence, we had probably two more guys that were were close. Um, so we knew that we were going to get a good football player. They were all I drew a line on our top 100 of ones that we would be looking to trade back, trade up and um, it fell where we had a couple guys there in the sequence. So, we looked to potentially move back a little bit. There wasn't much interest right behind us where we felt comfortable in terms of the numbers. Um, so we just moved forward and we we love the player, so we we were excited about pressure is there in a situation where you need a day one starter to go in and then be able to land that guy, but just like the process of getting him, how do you feel in that? And what is it like as you start to see the way the board falls before you guys get on the clock? >> Yeah. Um, you try to stay true to the top guys on the board. Um, you know, there there's a couple situations where potentially could be in a position where we have starters, but we would have very similar to last year, right, with with Cole and Coulson. Um, it just happened for this one that the sequence landed right on a a need. Um, so he's going to have the ability to come in and compete for a starting role and obviously that's that's going to be an open spot. Um, where those guys are going to compete and the tape tells us he's going to have a really good opportunity to do that. Um but this was a really cool opportunity where again a need and best player available um fell the way that we needed it to >> this offseason you and Ben both talked about the need to get better >> um from the outside is there still a way to do that in your mind on day two of the draft and if you don't you just have to the guys in house >> yeah I think both of those things are true I think there's some opportunity of guys uh on the board still um and then absolutely just what these guys are working on this week uh was for that group to continue to get better so they can be more effective. Um I know the coaches spent a lot of time in the offseason detailing where uh spots where they feel like we can get better, maybe some tweaks in what we're doing um the way we're coaching things. Um and then naturally just a second year in the system, you would think that some of these guys would continue to get better and elevate their game. And then if you if you help the secondary, like you know, they're related to a degree. Obviously, uh the Dline helps uh the back end more often than not. Uh but in a situation where, you know, we have good corners, good safeties, uh we can be in a position where maybe we can have the quarterback hold the ball a little longer. >> Did the edge rushers kind of break the way you thought they would? >> Yeah. Considering the the combination of of Kobe and Dylan and the speed you added back there, what does what strikes you about you do with those two guys and how fast they are? >> Yeah, I think you just match up better. Um, you eliminate, you know, every time we especially like our pro staff when we do an advance on our opponent. We're looking for targets, looking for guys that we can find mismatches on and expose. So, when you have speed and you have a lot of guys that can cover in different spots, um your ability to hang in there, cover longer while you're bringing pressure, uh things like that enhances the entire defense. >> Mentioned with the combination of Kobe and Dylan that there's no weaknesses between the two of them because they can do everything. What does that do for a defense when you're secondary? I mean, that would just point to the secondary being the strength of this defense. What can that do in year two with Dennis having that? >> Yeah, that group can elevate. Obviously, there's a lot of turnovers. um you can increase that number which is going to be you know a big challenge for those guys but I think just like I said taking the air out uh anytime we've seen a defense and you feel like like it's suffocating uh because of the speed um that's what we're trying to do >> right he he goes from Purdue to Oregon where did you see the most development like why does he really take off once that changes made >> yeah um you know there's plenty I mean you can mature uh continue to grow in just your understanding of the game. Um getting bigger, stronger, faster, different schemes, coaches. So, there's a lot of things that could potentially go into that. Um you know, he his first year as a freshman, I think he had six interceptions and was really really active, too. Um so, when we worked through all of his tape, there's a lot of things that popped up from the time he his first year to his last year. >> Brad talked about the football character. How did that jump out to you throughout the process of getting to know him? Yeah, it's off the charts and we we have so many good sources in terms of um guys that he's played with and that that's all the way from Westfield High School all the way to Oregon and the feedback that we got was incredible. Um I think um one of our guys probably Brett came down to talk to you and I don't know if he mentioned it but you know we had talked about this as a very similar type person player combination to what Coulson was. Um the work ethic um again that passion for ball was off the charts. We grade on a scale 1 to nine. Um there's no fives and there's no twos. Uh cuz I don't want there's no fence grades. U there's a lot of sevens and eights when you look across this guy's character. So u really happy with the type of person we're bringing in. Is it the combo of football character and kind of the speed that that makes you feel good about a safety in round one where there aren't a lot of them that go in round one and you can often times find pretty good ones a little bit later on in the draft when you think about positional value. >> Yeah, you got to look at versatility. So if it's a safety and it's like kind of old school box safety um that maybe doesn't have a lot of coverage um you know value probably stays down just a little bit. So that's why we felt comfortable taking Dylan where he was. There's versatility. So there's multiple positions he can play on top of the ability to cover the range helping in the pass game third down. Um and then when you have you got Kyler, you got Kobe, you got guys that you can do a lot of different things to confuse the defense. Um that was kind of on the checklist of a safety taking in one and grading them where we had him graded. >> Ryan Ben has complimented safeties in the past like during the season. like what was his reaction? What was his input? I thought >> Yeah, he was he was fired up. Um we spent time together. He would come in watch watch tape with with our group and this was one of the guys that we had on when he was in and I mean we both I can now feel Ben like he doesn't have to say anything. I can feel his like body language start to like get excited about somebody and you could you could feel it. Um because again it's that style of play that he he he has that like I said it's contagious. It's It's the type of um player that we want on our football team. >> Is there anything that surprised you from the first round tonight? >> Um yeah, but I'm not going to get into other people's picks. >> Walk off pick at Penn State as a signature play. What struck you about just the the moment and the actual play that he made in? >> Yeah, we we want players that can rise to the level. Um we plan on playing a lot of big games moving forward. We're going to I don't know what the schedule is going to be, but I'm sure there's going to be a lot of prime time games. There's going to be um hopefully we're back and deep into the playoffs. So, we need guys that thrive in those moments. Uh so, when you show those things, um we feel even better about you. >> When you look at your board heading into tomorrow and the three picks that you have, how do you feel about your needs and and the way things kind of shift out? >> Yeah. Uh a lot of good options. A lot of good options. Um, I'll say this, this was probably the most aggressive we were in terms of the guys that we really like. Like, they have to play our style. Um, they got to have the right makeup. Um, in terms of our scheme fits, like all of that had to be there. If it wasn't there, you're off the board. Um, we were really aggressive with it. So, when you look at it, it feels really thin. Um, but that's a good thing. I think it's a really good thing because we're very selective of who we want. Um there's some historical numbers that I have that makes me feel confident that um there's going to be guys that we like still available to us. So thankfully the numbers are high enough where you know I'll be able to sleep a little bit tonight. So >> what put you guys in that what put you guys in that space to be more aggressive? Is it the clear vision from the coaching staff? Is it the process the point you are in the process of roster building? >> I would say both. Both um just confident confidence in our system. Um, and then again, this staff is unbelievable. We're just giving clarity. And I think as as we continue to work with each other, we're going to know exactly what we're looking for. Um, so why why mess around with, you know, those that don't fit what we're trying to do and then we're, you know, then we're having conversations in, you know, the summertime and in the fall of why that guy can't play for us or, you know, it's not a fit. So, um, yeah, I think both things are true. just confidence in the system. Our scouts do unbelievable job gathering information and then our staff is our coaching staff is really clear with what they're looking for. So, it's a really good marriage. >> I know these guys are are kind of versatile, but do you see Kobe as strength at free and and feeling and strong or need to do a lot of matching based on coverages? Well, I think now, and that's probably a better question for DA, but I'm sure depending on who we're going against, um, he can do different things. Probably makes everything look the same, but do different things out of it. Um, which as offense is is difficult to prepare for. >> Awesome. Thank you. Thank you all.

title: Dillon Thieneman bringing speed to Bears defense | Press Conference
text: Hey Dylan, uh, welcome to Chicago. Congratulations. Uh, what was your pre-draft process like with with the Bears, uh, getting to know Ryan Ples and Ben Johnson, and what do you know about the franchise before that? >> Um, so my pre-draft process really at the combine, I had a a formal with them that went really well. Um, I feel like I really connected with all the guys there. Um, and then I hadn't talked to them too much, but I knew that they had a lot of interest in me. So, um, that was kind of most of the the conversations that we had. And, uh, I mean, I know I know a little bit about the Bears history. Like, I grew up not too not too far away from Chicago. So, um, I know I know a decent amount there. >> Dan, >> Dylan, uh, how do you kind of recap your interception against Penn State and and kind of what that was as a signature moment for you? >> Uh, that that moment I think was just incredible. like the way to to to seal the game like that was amazing and just do it for the team. Um we've been talking about that same play uh from like a defensive aspect like the play call and then that offensive formation like we've we've repped both of those together in practice and for it to show up in the game um just how the coaches kind of predicted was amazing. >> You've talked about kind of your recognition being a strength of yours. How do you strengthen that over the course of your your playing life and how did it get to the level it's at now? Um really just when I keep improving my process and my preparation like how I watch film um and taking notes, writing stuff down. So I had I had two separate notebooks. So I had a notebook just for opponent scout and I had a notebook where I wrote everything down. So I write everything in one notebook and then I would kind of compile it and what I needed to study, what I needed to know in another one so I could study that um before the game. >> Kevin, >> hey Dylan, congratulations. Um, a lot of the coaches have talked about your versatility. Uh, how did you kind of hone that and what are all the different positions you you kind of can see yourself helping out uh the Bears in? >> Um, well, I mean, at Purdue, I played mostly in the post, so I was playing free safety there, but then Oregon, we played field and boundary. And in Oregon's defense, you're asked to do literally everything. So, um, I mean, I'm rolling down in the box. I'm rotating different cover threes. I'm playing the half. I'm playing quarters. So I I got really comfortable playing a lot of different uh coverages and different positions. So I really good uh playing field and then I could play boundaries. So doing those and then I cross trainined nickel um in the offseason too. So I felt I felt pretty comfortable moving between all those positions because I I knew everything on the the back end. >> Courtney. >> Hey Dylan. The Bears have made a pretty big emphasis this offseason by adding speed to their defense. Um, I know you ran a 435 530. So, like two-part question here. Was that the time that you was that a goal time? Was that faster than you expected? And what do you think that speed can do to bring how do you feel like you can bring your speed to the NFL and how it translates to the NFL game? >> Uh, going into the combine training, I set a goal of being 4-3. Um, and then to go out there and do that kind of surpassed even my expectations at that point. Like, I knew I knew in my heart I was going to get 4-3. Um, but I didn't know what exactly it would be. Um, and I feel like speed is very very interesting because there's there's normal speed and then there's gameplay and speed. So the more you can process and recognize the faster you can play in game closer to your true speed. >> Sean, >> hey Dylan, congrats. Um, I'm wondering if you could just kind of take us through tonight. What is this whole experience like being there and and hearing your name? >> It's been incredible. I mean, it's it's a once in a lifetime moment. So, I'm very glad that I came here and got to experience that with the family and the other people that have helped me get to this point. >> Josh, >> hi. Welcome to Chicago. Uh, just curious how familiar you are with Dennis Allen and how you hear yourself as a playmaker. >> I'm sorry. Can you say that again? >> Yeah, sure. I was just wondering how familiar you are with Dennis Allen and how you hear yourself as a playmate or as a ball hawk in the secondary. Um, I'm not super familiar with Dennis Allen, but I'm sure we'll get to know each other quite well. Um, and then in the backhand and just really if I can utilize my speed, I can go get that ball. >> Dion, >> hi Dylan. Welcome. We're excited to have you. Um, you you mentioned just the journey that you've taken to go from Purdue and out to Oregon. Like, how how do you feel like you're prepared to take this NFL step and ready to kind of hit the ground running? I feel like making the the leap to to Oregon was kind of preparing me for the next level already. Like I'm going to a new place, new coaches, new scheme, new environment. Um, so I'm kind of used to that change and I know how to make it um and what works for me and what doesn't. So I'm kind of able to to grow from that last experience and um I think hit the ground running. >> Last two. Dan, >> Dylan, two quick ones. What's the uh the chain you got on and who gave that to you? Uh, we got the Bears chain and then someone in the crowd gave it to me when I went out and took a pick with the fans. >> Okay. Also, I know you've you've referenced Palamalo as a guy that you looked up to. What What drew you to his game when you were younger? >> Really, his versatility and um I liked watching some of his interviews like if he knew where the ball was going, he would go switch positions with that player so that he could be in on a play so he could have an impact for the team. So, just having that knowledge of the defense, but then also the understanding what the offense is trying to do. Last one, Courtney. >> Dylan, really quick, back to your speed. Have you always been fast? Is this something that like as a kid you realize like I'm just faster than everybody else? Is this something you had to really work on? >> I have always been fast, but I feel like it's really kind of picked up being in college. Um, I know my brothers would joke. I used to like race down the driveway all the time, like racing them or racing like the car on the way home from school, like some of that stuff. >> Awesome. Thank you so much, Dylan. Congratulations. >> Oh, thank you. >> We'll see you tomorrow.

title: Vega Ioane Introductory Press Conference | Baltimore Ravens
text: I'll be pretty quick here. Um, obviously super excited to get Vang in here and and uh be able to welcome him and his family to uh the Ravens family and and what was really clear, you know, obviously we get to spend time with a lot of different prospects in this this process. Um, but when he got to come in here and and we got to spend some time with him, it was very clear that uh he was a Raven and and what that meant, I mean, what that means to us is really um he embodies, you know, the idea, the values, all the things that uh we're looking to uh put into place here with Jesse and in the new regime. And um it was very clear to us that he would make a great uh addition to the the roster and be able to come in here. You know, he's he's a humble guy um that competes. He he shows it all over the tape and uh I'm certainly very excited to to be able to coach him and and uh him join us on on this uh journey here. >> Uh any questions for for either of us? >> Uh you know, welcome to uh Baltimore. Uh uh I we sort of asked you yesterday a little bit. How much you know because you'll be blocking in front of Lamar, how much have you kind of admired him from afar? And you know, so you know, now a day since you've been drafted, have you kind of thought about the the possibility of, you know, blocking for him as well? >> Oh man, I thought about it a lot. You know, his name is a big name around the game. He's been around the game for a little while now. He's a very talented player, phenomenal player. You know, it's going to be a big honor for me and a blessing for me to, you know, block for somebody like that. So, taking a lot of pride in that. >> Um, you brought up the, um, Alo aircraft, the Ali Natada, um, comparison. You said you've heard that before. Just curious, how familiar are you with him and and what does that kind of mean to you when you hear that? >> I'm familiar with his game. Um heard his name growing up, you know, watched a little bit of ball. His name was always around, you know, but being compared to somebody like that, it's not something to take lightly. You know, he's a great player. He's done a lot for the game himself. So, you know, to be compared to somebody like that means a lot to me. D, have you been able to kind of catch up to how fast pace it's probably been for you over the last 12 hours or so? >> Uh, not really. Uh, been a long day yesterday. Got about like 4 hours of sleep last night. Now we're here, but you know, all of it's a blessing. Know God has a plan for all of us, you know, just a part of it. You know, take not taking it lightly, but it's part of the process. >> How much uh do you know about the Ravens and their I know you've been asked a bunch of questions, but how familiar are you at? How much have you followed the team growing up? >> Um, I mean, I know the basics, you know, there's a lot of history, a lot of, you know, legends that came came through here. A lot of big names, know, a lot of, um, you know, legends that have left a big part of themselves into this facility, you know, a lot of this this game. So, it means a lot to me that I'm here now. >> Hey, Dean. Uh, something that Jesse mentioned last night is that the bank is really sche versatile and can fit in multiple different uh, schemes. How big of a factor was that during the evaluation process that made you want to to try to get in? >> That's a huge factor. I mean, obviously, um the versatility that he has in his game, it allows you on offense to be very multiple and um you know, really he can do a lot of different things and and you always want to be building the scheme around the player. Um and because of his unique skill set, it allows you to uh be able to try to stress defenses in a lot of different ways. Exactly. What we heard a little bit about it, but what was Coach Leford like to be around last night when the fake came in and how much did he push for this? >> So, like you you got to see the video of um you know, Eric being able to talk and Jesse being able to talk. You couldn't see Coach Led walk into the room and just like jumping out of his seat like ready to explode. So, um Coach Leadford was so fired up from the very beginning. Um, you know, we really identified Vanga as a guy that really we really felt like would uh add to our offense and um he's been beating that drum for for weeks now. Um, for it to be able to come to fruition and you know him to be sitting there when we were picking um it was it was really just uh awesome for for all sides. >> And can you talk about your relationship already that you're starting to build with coach Leadford and I I know he was working you out at your pro day and kind of how how that all went with him. >> Yeah, that was the first time I met him. you know, he's explaining the drills and then I had a rep like I'm up taking a knee about to run outside zone. He goes, "I'mma hold a bag." I was like, "All right, I'm going to use that to my advantage." You know, I'm trying to push him on his ass a little bit, you know, and then after the entire, you know, we're done with proday, he comes up. He's like, you almost put me on my ass. I was like, you know, trying to play it off like I didn't know I was trying to do that. So, but, you know, that's my guys. This is how the game works, you know? So, >> thank you. There's always going to be some people who say, "How do you take a guard in the first round, right? Why why don't you take a pass rusher or what have you. What if anything would you say to those people? >> There's, you know, 11 people on the field at the same time. You're missing one. You can't play a game of football. You can't play real football without O linemen. And if you don't have a complete five, there's five people up front that play as one. There's a lot of pride that needs to be taken upon that. So for me getting picked first round to play as a guard, take a lot of pride in that. coming in. I'm trying to, you know, make a big impact playing as a guard, just proving them wrong. >> Thing after you heard your name called and got drafted, what is kind of the coolest and most memorable thing that happened since? Was it a moment you share with your family? Was it a phone call you got? What would you say was the kind of the one thing that really stuck out since you got drafted? >> Um, I say two big moments. When I put the hat on my dad, he didn't take it off for the next like two hours. He left the hat on the entire time. And after that, we took a picture as a whole family. You know, I got eight siblings. I'm the ninth and youngest one. We're all standing there, you know, nice little view in the back. It's my entire family. That's my whole reason of being here, making it this far. You know, those people are my my why. Like I said before, you know, I did this for them. And seeing that come to fruition, like you said, that's that's a big part to me. >> Then as you're growing up and developing and, you know, the possibility of being an NFL player comes into focus. Who were some offensive linemen and some players that maybe you watched, you studied, that you modeled yourself after that made an impression on you? >> I was a big Quentyn Nelson fan. Watched a lot of his film, a lot of Zion Johnson film. Um, I say Peter from Titans, the Titans as well, a lot of those film and uh Trent Williams, I watch a lot of his film as well. He's I know he's a tackle, but he plays real well. >> And I know you were a rugby player growing up predominantly. When was it that you kind of fell in love with football? Can you tell us the story or the moment that you kind of realized it? >> I mean, I watched a lot of football growing up. My older brothers, they w or they play football high school and all that. And I was a young kid watching them play on the islands and, you know, didn't really not much came from that with them. But, you know, from then on, I knew the game was a big part of our family, our culture, things like that. Came to Washington State, you know, my mom said no football, no nothing like that. Focus on school. She's right here, but you know, she loves football now and that's all that matters to me. >> When Jesse said yesterday that you guys still don't really know yet how the guard configuration is going to work out, what is that figuring out process look like to you? >> Yeah, I mean really with the offensive line always, it's how do we get up five best on the field? Um obviously he's got a lot of versatility and and that allows us to really um go out and try to explore that through the offseason, through training camp and uh really make it a competitive environment that um you know our guys are able to kind of showcase their skill sets where we think they're going to fit our offense best um and be able to make that decision you know later on into camp. But um certainly guys like this that have you know a lot of different they've played a lot of different places. Um, I mean, I've seen him flexed out as a tight end at times and slicing back and and, um, you know, knocking out an end on the other side. And so, um, guys like that allow you to, uh, really explore, you know, what is the best fit for our our best five. >> Have you found that guys earlier in their career are typically more flexible when it comes to moving from the left side to the right side and vice versa? >> I would say, yeah, I mean, just muscle memory for anybody, um, the more reps you take on anything, the more comfortable you get there. And um so you know really a transition time like this where he's coming from uh college to pro you know that is uh it's a really good time to to make that change if you're if you're moving around. >> One of the stats that kind of jump out about him that you know hasn't allowed a sack the last two years at Penn State you know and watching him. What makes him so good as a pass protector? >> Uh reactive athleticism is um of a very very strong trait. He's great with his hands. um he does a great job of of starting the fight in in the rush. Um I think there's a a lot of different reasons that uh that stat comes out. It's not one one area of his game. There's a lot of areas of his game where uh he does a great job of controlling the depth of the pocket and being able to uh you know handle whether that's a guy playing outside of him or or a guy playing in the A gap. Um he does he does a great job in protection. >> Um when you got the call and heard it was the Ravens, what was the first thing that came to mind? And since then, have you had any uh current Ravens reach out to you? >> Um, no current Ravens reach out yet. You know, I'm expecting it, but you know, I was talking to EDC before I left. He goes, like right before I'm walking out the building, he goes, "When you get that call with that uh area code, you know, it's going to be us." My phone's sitting there, I see the area code pop up. You know, I just felt a whole, you know, feeling of relief. You know, everything just flushed out and I relaxed a little bit knowing that that moment was everything that I've been working for. I got the call, answered it, I said, "What's up, big dog?" We're ready to go. You know, things like that. But I was real happy that I'm here now. Ben, >> I was reading uh maybe a year or two ago, you dropped about 20 pounds going into a season. Uh what did that do for your game? And do you consider maybe like your athleticism as well as your strength to be, you know, one of one of your strengths? >> Uh for me, it definitely improved my level of play. um felt like I was moving a lot quicker, coming off the ball more, just being lighter. But the whole losing weight thing, it was more of just a me decision. After the season, my junior season, I was like, "Let me see what 325 feels like." Personally, I didn't feel like I lost any power or anything like that. But, you know, my old line coach is saying that I'm moving a lot better. You know, just playing ball better. So, >> good. What um what's your earliest I know you said you grew up, you know, go out and see watching your older brothers play. What's your earliest just general football memory and what app kind of appealed to you? >> Um, I say 10th grade. Got my first start on varsity. I'm playing left tackle. We're playing a team from Oregon. You know, he's he's like six. I've never seen somebody that big. You know, he's coming off the ball. He beats me off the edge and I'm grabbing him and I'm pulling it back as he's beating me off the edge. I had no idea what I was doing, but got a flag caught on me, but you know, that's how it was. Hey, what's the uh best worst pronunciation you've heard of in your name? >> Oh man. Um, for some reason I don't understand where people get the L from in my last name. They spell with an L, but somebody spelled my name Oliva Vanga or something like that. Y oron. It's no good, but I hope you would get it now. So, >> I remember there's an interview that you said you learned pretty quick how to be physical when going up against uh Penn State defensive lineman and pass rushers. Was it Diesa Isaac one of them or does it mean to be teammates with him now? >> Diesa Isaac back then, you know, we had crazy different packages on defense and I was like a two at the time. You know, he's lined up at the four eye and his get off is insane. Like he was he was an athlete back then. He still is now. with his his like hand grip. I remember punching him one time. He grabs my hand with like barely any effort into it and just rips it off of him. He like beats me off that I get ripped by my line coach. So that's how it was going against him. >> There was a story when you were in college about you used to print out pictures and sticky notes of other teams, guys, and put them on your bedroom wall just to remind you. Where did that start? Where did that come from? How did that help? And is that something you might try to do in the NFL? Uh for me it was a lot of like changing my process of how I get ready for a game. Um that started like late junior season. It was more of a thing reminding me that that's the goal of the entire week. You know, reminding myself that these are the guys I'm going against, you know, drilling in my head, you know, what they do, how they play, things like that. But it's all part of the process of getting ready for the next game. >> People who review your film talk about just the consistency of the pass block reps. I mean, the the efficiency of the movement, the the lack of penalties, all that kind of when when did you and how did you sort of become that technician? >> Um, it's a big shout out to my O line coach. You know, that was one thing he harped on a lot was being detailed as an O lineman. It was either being detailed in the meeting room or out on the field. It's all the focusing on, you know, technique stuff, getting your hands here rather than there, things like that. Getting your your foot there on in the run game. But now, I focus a lot on the little details rather than the big things. So, >> can you uh I guess take us through the process of of getting that suit and what what it means to you? >> I just wanted to keep it simple and the lapel is just like part of our culture, you know, get a little tribal on there, but nothing much to it. >> Yesterday, you talked about kind of how you flipped that switch from off the field to on the field instead. It took you a while to kind of perfect that. Was that, you know, kind of ramping yourself up into that intensity and that mindset? like can you talk about that process of kind of be building that that flip of the switch? >> Uh for me pregame I'm going in, you know, calm. You can't do nothing full speed when you're, you know, all all antsy and things like that. So I'm all calm during the game or before the game. As soon as the game starts, you know, I'm a different person. I'm trying to kill somebody. But, you know, it's all staying calm and then when you see me play on the field, it's it's calm as well. But the mentality of just talking smack, things like that. No, I'm confident in my preparation, knowing what's going on before it happens. That's why I play like that. >> Bang. You talk to your um your old quarterback Josh. You told me about story about you guys playing that game against Collins Hill and the bus being surrounded and you kind of standing up and and and you know saying I got this and taking everybody off. What do you remember about that moment? What kind of prompted you to to be the guy in that situation? I mean, not much to it, you know, just showing up, you know, being the guys that do the things that nobody else wants to do. I take a lot of pride in that. Um, you know, I was one of those guys that everybody looked up to. But, you know, I'm never a guy that speaks before, you know, things need to be said, but, you know, when things need to be said, I'll definitely be the guy to do it. >> Man, if somebody ask you what's the best and the worst part of growing up being the youngest of nine, what would you say? Um, excuse my language, but they used to beat my ass all the time. That's that's how bad it got. But, you know, they they roughed me up a little bit growing up, but that's just how the household was. You know, like I said, I wouldn't be here if it wasn't for them. So, >> are you the biggest now? >> No. >> Yeah. I got brothers that are bigger than me. So, >> yeah. >> All right. All right. Thank you. It was coming.

title: Eric DeCosta: 'Vega Ioane Checked Off Every Box' | Baltimore Ravens
text: guys. I think it was a successful start to our draft. Very excited to get Wena here in Baltimore. He's a guy that we've studied at length. We had a chance to spend some time with him at the combine and also um here in Baltimore at length. Great, great kid, excellent player. Obviously have a lot of ties to the Penn State football program. Had the chance to watch him play a couple years at both left and right uh guard. Physical uh tough, very athletic for his size, excellent in pass protection, a great fit for our offense and what we're trying to accomplish. Um and we're just very very happy to have him here. So, um questions. >> Eric, when it came to 14, because there were a couple surprises up there for you guys. Uh, did you consider it an easy decision once you looked at the board? What were you going with? >> Uh, you know, I wouldn't say it was easy decision. Uh, you know, there were certainly some really good players still available, guys that we really liked quite a bit. Um, but in the end, I think as we looked at it and just talked to our scouts and our coaches especially, we felt that Wenger was the best pick for us. >> Eric, did you have interest in that pick? Was were you weighing any trade uh possibilities when you were at the clock? Um we we did get a call that just kind of ended up just falling apart. Um we did consider potentially a trade back, but it had would have to have made sense for us based on the players still available and the amount of players that we really wanted at that spot. So for us to go back basically we would have had to ensure that we would have gotten one of a handful of players. Um it didn't really materialize at the end and the other team decided they wanted to make the pick and clarified things for us. It was easy for us to turn the card in at that time. >> Jesse, your first term as the head coach in that in that war room. What was your experience like tonight? >> It was great. Um, I mean, these guys do a phenomenal job and we, you know, I think between the coaches, the front office, we all put a lot of work into evaluating players and kind of figuring out what we're looking for. Um, you know, the guy that we got, I think, as a first pick is is the epitome of what we want the team to be like. you know, line of scrimmage, dominant team. Uh, so really physical, really great player, really great person. Really enjoyed getting to know him a little bit on the visit and, uh, he's everything that we want our guys to be. >> Jesse, do you anticipate him being at left guard? >> I think we'll figure that all out. I mean, he's a great player. He's played he's actually played guard, both guards. He actually started one game at center a couple years ago. So, I think he's got a lot a lot of versatility and we'll figure out the best uh best way to get our best players on the field. >> Eric, when you look at how much you have invested in Lamar, how much you have invested in Henry, um do you feel like sort of um definitely I mean sort of investing even that investment so to speak in making sure that your backfield is protected. >> I think that's right. you know, we want to be a we want to be a strong imposing team and uh you know, we we probably haven't invested as many resources in the offensive line recently. Um I don't you I think other than probably uh Tyler Linderbomb, this is the first first round pick we've used in an offensive lineman probably since Ronnie Stanley. Before that, I believe probably Ben Grubs, maybe 2007, and we doubled up that year with Yonder and Grubs. So, I I think this guy just really checked off every single box for us as a player. Uh mentality, personality, ability, skill level, athletic ability, physicality, all those different things. Um at a at a very high level and uh you know, we love when we can get the best player at his position in the draft, which we've done a lot, and kind of take pride in that. Um so, we think he's a great fit for us and certainly going to help the players around him on the offensive line. uh they'll help him as well, but I think he's going to make us better and really make the middle of our offense very strong. >> Jesse, I know you guys have spent extensive time with with him and other prospects, but I guess the first time we got to meet him, he described himself big described himself as a mer and he specifically said, "I'm not going to let anyone touch my quarterback." I guess just with this being your first night as head coach, what's your reaction to that? Does it give you a charge on? >> Yeah, that gives me a real charge. um you know that's when you when you meet him and you get to know him that's his mentality but he also has like this humility about him which kind of uh just sparks like how hard he works and he doesn't he doesn't assume that he's going to be a great player. He puts in the work and the time um and just really man just couldn't be more excited to add his mentality the way that he plays his play style really matches what we're trying to do. Jesse, what did Dwayne Leford? What was his reaction and what was his evaluation? What he had to say about the video? >> I think coach Leadford was pretty excited. Uh there may be a video that comes out at some point where you'll see his reaction. Uh but he was very excited. Obviously, he uh is a guy that we put a lot of time in the eval process. Um probably, you know, very very very very high up there on coach Sledford's list of favorite players in the draft and uh worked out for us. Eric, you you love the misdirection before the draft and not being predictable. Were you concerned in the days ahead of this draft that so many people were connecting you to uh Wenger that it might he might get away from you and teams would trade up in front of you to get him? >> You know, you're always a little concerned. You're not you're not really sure, especially where there's some teams picking in front of us that know us pretty well. Um kind of similar last year with Starks, I think. Um, but in the end, you know, we just kind of stick to the board and and let the board fall to us, which is something I learned from Azie many years ago. And uh, you know, sometimes it works out, sometimes it doesn't. And if it hadn't worked out, we had other players that we would have picked, excellent players. So, I thought I I said we were in a good spot um, leading up to the draft and it sort of played out that way for us for what we wanted to accomplish with our team, with our roster. There were several players that really would have fit us this year and helped make us a better football team. Fortunately, we got one of our favorite guys. >> Go ahead. Sorry. Go ahead. >> Were you surprised Bane was still there that he fell, >> you know, he's a great player, too. Um, and you know, and I think, uh, you know, a player that, you know, again, another guy, he's, you know, a great selection by the Bucks, I think would have made a great Raven. You know, those are the tough decisions that we have to make. Um, but in the end, I really feel like we got a guy that really fits us personalitywise and abilitywise and just everything that we want our guys to be. I think, you know, Venga kind of epitomizes that and we're excited to see what he can do. >> Eric, um, you've touched on this a little bit. Steve mentioned obviously back in January. Um, you know, best player available, but but did you feel like offensive line was really the most important need for you guys and to address that really early on? I >> I mean, I think is definitely one of the one of the positions that we we prioritized. there were some others and there are some others and we'll continue to hopefully have a chance to address those players. I need some more picks, you know, cuz there's some good players that are going to be available, but uh we do hope to, you know, definitely attack some other position groups as well. Um I think that just, you know, when you think you're good with the roster, things happen, right? And so we want to be strong at every position with as much depth as possible. And uh that's why we're excited, I think, about the next couple days and the amount of picks that we have and the opportunities that present themselves. Eric, I mentioned I think in the first round tonight, nine offensive line were taken. How good has what, you know, in just going leading up to this draft, how good did you think this offensive line class was? >> I mean, I think very deep. Very deep. And and the fact is, you know, there's still some really good players. I mean, normally if you saw nine players going any given round, you would think that it was going to thin out really quickly. And I think still now looking at that those positions, there's still some excellent football players available. And I I think it speaks to the cyclical nature of the draft. Every year there's different positions that are strong and other positions maybe not quite as strong. Last year happened to be, you know, defensive line was really strong. Um this year I think offensive line certainly one of the better positions in the draft and I think the other teams to recognize that as well. >> Eric, you mentioned that you feel that uh Venga is best at his position in this draft. >> Um you know relative to other guards, I mean did you feel something about his ceiling and his, you know, technical ability or physical gifts >> made it important to get the best guy at guard relative to other guards in the draft. I know that might be complicated because you might draft more guards here. >> Yeah. So, for me, a big thing is just watching the tape and evaluating and seeing everything, how the guy does all those testing and things and talking to people. But a big part of the process for me is really meeting with the players. And that's really a way for me to, you know, separate these guys. I mean, you know, I've been blessed to be here 30 years and I can't imagine how many players I've met, but you start to build up a bank of memories and different interviews and different players and things. And meeting him uh was impressive and uh left an impression with me. He reminds me, and I told him this and he laughed. He said because somebody else has told him this, he reminds me a little bit of one of my favorite Ravens of all time, Hodata. uh and just the way that he was with me in the office and we were talking and laughing and his maturity um and the way that he even though he's a younger person, even the way that he carried himself with a quiet confidence stood out. So, you know, uh in the end, as you're trying to split all these guys up, because these guys are all really good players, they're the best in the world and what they do in college football. In the end, these these interviews and these visits, they end up really kind of beingcoming the nuance of how you kind of split hairs with these guys. I mean, you you've talked about some of the challenges of taking a guard in the first round because of the fifth year valuation aspect of it. Um, >> so to take a guard that high, I mean, do you do you essentially have to believe that that could be a Pro Bowl player, that it could be one of the best guys in the league at that position? >> I mean, that would be the hope, you know, that would be the goal. I think that we have seen the the guard market start to mirror more of the tackle market. Uh, we saw this year the center market trying to catch up. I think you know teams people are realizing that these offensive linemen are special athletes who who do very unique things. Um they're hard to find and so that market has grown and changed and and will adjust with it. But again um I firmly believe that this guy is going to be a really really good player with us for the next five years and hopefully longer than that. Um there are obvious obviously challenges um with the way that that offensive line kind of frarier option is all kind of encompassed with tackles, guards, and centers. But I'm not going to worry about that today. That's something for me to worry about three years from now. >> Eric, beyond just, you know, fortifying and pass protection and how important was it to get someone who could be a people mover in the run game because, you know, we know just how much of those running lanes for Derek only amplified his talents. I mean, I think that's been, you know, a hallmark of the Ravens over the last seven years is the ability to run the football and and be a physical downhill team that can just take over games and crunch time in the fourth quarter and put teams away. And so, uh, I think I think Vanar really fits that mentality in the way that he plays. And I think, um, I think it's a really good fit for us in terms of what we like to be up front. And, uh, I think our fan base is going to love them, too. >> Eric, I know you like look for every piece of little information. There there was a viral video of him like leaping over and I saw >> that. Does that leave an impress? Does that even >> Yeah. I mean, you know, those things we we look at all that stuff, you know. I think, you know, there was another player that uh I I watched his high school wrestling videos. Um all that stuff matters in some little small way, you know, and so yeah, I saw that he helps the guy push the thing. Yeah. Yeah, that was really cool. Um I think it speaks to his humility and uh just who he is as a person, how his parents raised him, for sure. Um but yeah, I mean all that stuff we look at all that social media, you know, I always tell my kids be careful because people like me are scouring the internet looking at your social media, you know. Um so yeah, I think that stuff's really important. >> Jesse, what um just from a technical football standpoint, what stood out to you most about it? >> You know, I think like especially with a guard, he's not he's not scheme dependent. So this guy could run any type of run scheme, any type of pass blocking scheme. It's not like, well, he, you know, he fits in a scheme where they turn and run or he fits in a scheme where they double team people. He can do all that. And he also lined up as a offthe- ball tight end with motion and knock people out, you know, slice blocking and things like that. So, I just think the the versatility to really do everything at a really high level, his athleticism, and then I think when you watch the tape, his play style and his play demeanor, you can sort of feel like he's really trying to, you know, block these guys like really really with a with the right mindset. And so, I think all that really jumps off when you watch this tape. Eric, just touching on another piece of news. Uh Zay Flowers, a two-time pro bowler for you. Was it important for you guys to um pick up his fifth year option and ideally would you like to see an extension uh done at some point in in the future? >> Yeah, for sure. I mean, I actually was shocked you guys didn't ask me about that at the uh draft press conference. The first time in how many years, Jameson? It's been a while, you know. Um but what I I would of course I would have told you guys. Uh no, we're fired up. Um I love Zay. He's he's he's earned this. Uh he's a tremendous player with a great work ethic and a great personality. Infectious, very talented. He's a leader and uh the goal would be to get along to him, deal with him if we can, and I I fully expect we will. >> He's got a great agent and he's a he's a great person. I know he wants to be >> My apologies. Um Eric, there were reports a few days ago that Naomi Matabk underwent surgery last week. Um focus on the draft, but just anything you can share about that and the idea that you guys might be hopeful he'll be able to play. Yeah, you know, um there's not much I can say. Uh I will say Nambi's here, you know, he is here in the build. Not tonight, but he's here now um in the program, offseason program. Um but you know, uh that's internal business. It's his business. If he wants to say anything about anything, he's more than welcome to. But as a club, I think our policy is to protect the players and not have any kind of statements regarding their health or anything personal like that. Um, but he is here and he's going to be here as far as I know. Um, and we're excited about that. >> Okay. >> Thank you.

title: RB Jeremiyah Love Press Conference | AZ Cardinals
text: All right, good morning everybody. Uh, thank you guys all for coming out. I know it was a a quick turn after last night. Um, none quicker than the uh, gentleman off to my left here and the the crew sitting sitting down here in front. So, uh, before we get going and and turn it over to Jeremiah, who that's the one you're all here to talk to, um, just want to welcome a few people. Um, you know, Jeremiah has got his family in town here, his mom and dad, uh, Jason and Latana, uh, sister Jayla and girlfriend Unique. Um, you know, we got some some flowers for them. I just appreciate you guys and and, uh, what you've done to to get you Jeremiah here. [laughter] Hands off, Dad. Uh but again guys, we're we spoke last night a little bit. Um excited for you guys to get a chance to talk to Jeremiah um for for as good of a football player is on the field. Um and even better person off the field and you guys are going to find that out real quickly here. So, uh you know, you've heard enough from me already. I want to get Jeremiah up here and give you a chance to talk to him. So, newest member of the Arizona Cardinals, Jeremiah Love. [applause] Glad to be here, guys. Um, glad to see all you guys' faces. I'm looking forward to building great relationships with you all. Um, just want to thank you to, uh, Mr. Bidwell and, um, you know, everybody that's believed in me to, you know, let me allow me to stand here right now. Um, you know, thank you to God as well. Thank you to my family and um thank you to these special gentlemen over here for just giving me a chance. But um I'm ready to work. I'm here to work and uh thank you for believing in me and you want to do some great things. >> We will open up to questions. We have Mike with the microphone over here and in the middle. So just get their attention and if you don't mind just saying your name and your ailation. Richard signs. >> Jeremiah Richard signs Fox 10. Welcome to the Valley. Uh you know this is obviously a big day for you. a dream come true, I would imagine. Just tell us uh what it's like for not just you, but for your support system, your your family that's here, and that obviously means so much to you. >> Um it's everything to us, you know. Um we've worked so hard to get here. You know, we sacrificed a lot to get here. My mom and dad, you know, I've sacrificed a lot of their time. Um my mom and dad were police officers growing up, so you can only imagine how the household was. You know, my sister went to school to be a nurse, so she's always grinding. And then shoot, everybody just, you know, putting in to get me here. So, it's very it's a very special moment for us all and um we're very grateful for this opportunity and um like I said, I'm here to work and I'm ready to work and uh I'm going to make sure that I take advantage of every single opportunity that I get and uh we're going to do some great things. But we're all grateful for uh this moment and we're blessed to be here and the only reason we're here is because of God. >> Hey Jeremiah, Mark Mcclo, Arizona's family 3TV CBS 5. Welcome to the Valley. Hey, wanted to ask you specifically about uh ball security because you look at the numbers and you're able to hold on to the football. So, uh what's your philosophy when it comes to that? A lot of people talk about it, but how are you able to to execute holding on to it? And >> so, ball security is everything. You know, the ball is the game. You know, without the ball, you can't win games. So, um when I first got to college, my running back's coach, Da McCulla, um shoot right from the bat, you know, told me the importance of ball security. And I kid you not, in literally the stretch lines, my very first stretch line, he gave me like this beeper ball and I had to hold it throughout the whole stretch throughout the little whole little warm-up run and it had to be beeping the whole time. If it wasn't beeping, you got to redo everything. So, um, Coach McCulla is the first person, you know, when I came to college that emphasized the importance of ball security and it just stuck with me the whole way. And I'm sure you can see some pictures of me running the end zone with, you know, having the ball capped and, you know, that's what it's all about, protecting the football, protecting the quarterback. And you know, that's what I'm going to do as a running back, protect that ball and allow and and allow us to have uh success. >> Hey Jeremiah, I'm Josh Weinfest, ESPN. Last night you told us that you're on the hunt for something greater. Can you kind of expand on that? What is that something greater and what does that look like in the short term and the long term? >> So obviously me being drafted um number three to come to the Cardinals is a blessing. You know, it's a dream come true. But what I what I meant when I said I'm on the hunt for something greater is wanted to convey that I'm not complacent. You know, I'm not satisfied from just getting here. You know, I want to be a Hall of Famer by the end of my time playing. You know, I want to be one of the greatest running backs to come through the game. So, I'm always on the hunt for something greater. And then even after football, I'm on the hunt for something greater. You know, go back to school and get my degree. Um, I wanted to become a doctor before I played football. So, um, throughout life, I'm always going to be on the hunt for something greater. Um, and that's just me, you know, that's how I was raised. My mom and dad told me to never be complacent, never be satisfied. You know, Coach Freeman always says, you know, choose hard and consistently find ways to get better. >> Hey Jeremiah, Tyler Drake with Arizona Sports. Welcome to the Valley. Uh your Notre Dame running mate, first round pick as well going to Seattle. Uh what's the trash uh talk going to be like that? And what's it just mean to see uh your running mate go in the first round of Sue? >> It means everything. Literally JD was the first person that I texted, you know, once I got drafted and once I saw he got drafted and I got on my phone. JD was the first person that came to mind. You know, I've watched JD work for, you know, three years. You know, we've been together, you know, been we've been partnered up in that running back room for three years. So, I mean, it was everything to see him get drafted. You know, I seen him, you know, put in the work. You know, I seen him, you know, grind through the injuries and, um, for him to be able to get drafted and and go to a great team at that, you know, it was just a great moment. you know, I love seeing my guys have success. You know, that's going to be no different here. You know, I'm going to build great relationships with the players, with the coaches, you know, with the ownership and, you know, I want this organization to have success and I'm going to contribute to that. So, when I saw JD, you know, get drafted, it was just it was it was a very, very heartwarming moment and um I made sure I had to congratulate him on that. >> [snorts] >> Jeremiah Teraki, Arizona Republic. You talked yesterday about your favorite runs are the short yardage runs, but obviously your ability in the open field is is quite special as well. The ability to turn 10 into 80. Where does that come from for you, that that ability in the open field and at the second level? >> I would say it all starts from uh me um playing in high school. my uh head coach at the time uh his name is Scott Pingle um made sure that you know I practiced a certain way you know and that practice translated to the games and he always told me he loved my short yardage runs rather than uh my long run. So um in practice there was a huge emphasis on finishing and making sure you're being gritty and tough. Um and um the saying at at CBC was uh brick by brick. you know, you got to to build a to build a house or to build a a place of staying, you know, you got to start with a foundation. You got to build it up brick by brick. You got to be tough. So, um that's where the foundation was laid at CBC uh with Scott Pingle being my head coach and uh just telling me to make sure I'm practicing hard, make sure I'm being greedy and being a tough player. And then that translated over to college. You know, I had great coaches like Coach McCulla. I had a great, you know, offensive coordinator, Mike Denim Brock, and then I had a great head coach that consistently told me to, you know, be gritty, be tough, and, uh, be consistent. So, um, that's where I get it from. >> Jeremiah Darren Urban from acardinal.com. I'm curious, everybody who talks about you talks about what a great kid you are and how how well you handle yourself. Um, it also is very clear that you're a very confident person. I'm curious. You have all these people saying you're you were the best player in the draft. you have all this talent. How do you walk that line between trying to stay humble, but also having that confidence that comes with what you bring to the table? >> You know, it all just comes down to just being myself. You know, a lot of people say I'm confident. You know, a lot of people say I'm humble, but at the end of the day, I'm just being who I am. You know, and uh however that's portrayed, that's portrayed. Um but, you know, at the end of the day, I'm just here to work, man. I'm I'm I'm blessed to be here. I'm here to work. And uh that's how I've gotten here, and that's what I'm going to continue to do. you know, find ways to get better on the field and off the field and just be authentically me. So, um, thanks for saying I'm humble. Thanks for saying I'm confident, but, um, I'm just being myself, man, and and that's what I'm going to continue to be. >> Hi, Jeremiah. Robbie Baker with Fox 10. Welcome here to Arizona. I'm just curious what kind of running backs you enjoyed watching coming up and what running backs maybe you molded your game after over the years. >> Yeah. So, um, I didn't mold my game after anybody growing up. You know, I didn't watch football much. You know, my dad put on some Barry Sander highlights for me. You know, I like Barry Sanders. I I think of him as the best running back of all time. Um, but players that I've watched, you know, recently, Jir Gibbs, Seaquan, uh, Derek Henry, Christian McAffrey, um, Alvin Chimera, you know, those are all great backs. You know, I love their playing style. You know, Jir Gibbs is very quick. You know, he's very fast. You know, fast burst. And, um, you know, Chris McAffrey is recovery. It's great. You know, I got to talk with him not too long ago. got to pick his brains because uh my strength coach at Notre Dame, Lauren Landal, uh was known Christian his whole life. So, he connected me and him. Got to talk to him for a little bit and uh just he just, you know, advised me on what to do and how to be a pro coming into this league. Um and then Derek Henry, big guy, strong guy, teaches you how to run tough. And then Alvin Kimera, just the whole he got the whole toolbox. He can receive, he can block, he can run. So, I like to watch him for that. And then I think the other guy say what I say. Barry Sanders, it's the best running back of all time. [laughter] Yeah. >> Hey, Jeremiah. Uh, last night Michael Flores said that you don't have any weaknesses in your game as pass as a receiver, as a rusher, and and pass protection. What is about pass protection that I guess you enjoy, you embrace, and how do you balance working on that with kind of the other parts of your game? >> So, so pass protection is the most important part of my game. you know, that's probably the the most that's the only thing I really train on when I'm when I'm at practice. You know, footwork is is natural. We we do tuneups, but pass protection is what we really, you know, focus on because you got to be able to protect the ball. You got to be able to protect the quarterback so that he can have time to make plays. Um, and I mean, I like pass protection. I get to hit people. You know, people always hitting me. So, whenever I get to deliver a blow, you know, I'm I'm going to take pride in that and I'mma, you know, do the best of my ability to try to knock your head off. you know, if I get a, you know, a quarterback that is trying to run, I'm going to make sure I clear a path for him, you know, and put my body on the line for that. So, um, I love pass protection. You know, I love trying to hit people. You know, I'm a football player end of the day. I used to play defense back in the day. So, um, I got a little bit of craziness to me, you know. So, pass protection is is key for success. >> Jeremiah Cameron, Cox, 12 News. Welcome to the Valley. I think Paris Johnson Jr. agrees with that statement. Uh what does it mean to have some of your teammates here to support you today? And then what most excites you about joining the Cardinals? >> Just uh being able to build a brotherhood. You know, obviously I got Perez, I got Marv here. Um they took the time out of their day to come and see me and that means a lot. You know, that shows that, you know, there's a brotherhood at uh here at the Cardinals. And I'm just happy to be, you know, uh being able to be a part of that. you know, I plan to come in and and build a great relationship with these guys, get to know them more um because, you know, they just know me on a service level. You know, I want to get to know them more as people off the field and um that's what I plan to do coming in. Um but it means the world to me to see these guys come in here and just, you know, show their faces because at the end of the day, they didn't have to do that, but they did. So, that just shows me the great culture that's here at the Cardinals, and I plan to come in, you know, make that culture better. >> Jeremiah, Zack Gershman, a carinal.com. Good to see you again. Uh yesterday you were talking a ton about competing. What is it specifically about competing that you enjoy the most? >> Just being able to compete against great players, you know. Um I've always been a competitor, you know, whether it's in football, whether it's in ping pong. See, they got a ping pong table in there. So I'm going to get I'm going to get with the guys on that. But I mean, I just like competing, you know, um at anything, you know. It could be football, it can be in the classroom, it can be in pingpong, it could be at swimming or whatever it may be. I'm just a competitor. Um, but as far as this league, the NFL is built up of the best players in the game. So, I'm excited to, you know, team up with great players like these guys over here and then also play against some great players. You know, I get to play against uh Jadarian Jadarian Price, you know, this upcoming season. He's a great player and I can't wait to, you know, do a little jersey swap with him, too. So, uh, I'm just excited to compete with great players and that's really what this is all about. >> Hey, Jeremiah, congratulations. Uh, David Brandt from the Associated Press. Um, you know, for whatever reason, the past 20 or so years, not many running backs have been drafted as high as you, but when they have been, you know, it's been guys like Saquon Barkley or Bejian Robinson who have had big impacts. What What do you think an elite running back can bring to a team and and why is that so important? >> Just that, you know, that ability to keep drives going. You know, you got to be able to do good and short yardage. You got to be able to score those tough touchdowns.
