It's about finishing and for anyone that's watched this young man's tape, you know, the highlight of his tape is how he finishes plays. It's something that's innate, something that's in him and something that we truly believe in here. And I know he's going to bring that toughness and that physicality and that finish mindset, that relentless mindset that we look for. He's bringing that to our team. So, that's why we're fired up to have him. This is for Nick and I guess maybe DeMeco a little bit. Nick, last night you mentioned some of the elements of the grade that you had on Keelan that were, you know, were really high. Can you kind of reveal without revealing too much about those elements specifically? Yeah, anytime you're creating a profile on a player, there's obviously the physical components on the field and then you look at some of the intangible items that are going to apply to the player from a coachability, from an intelligence standpoint, football character, instincts, toughness, overall competitiveness, the way DeMeco alluded to it. So, those are things like we prioritize in this program. We prioritize and every player is evaluated based on that criteria. And Keelan like stood head and shoulders above a lot of other players. So, that's a part of the evaluation. So, when you combine that with what you see on the tape, then you put the profile of the player together and say like this is what a Houston Texans football player looks like. So, we take a lot of pride and we put a lot of value in that. Like you guys have been around our team like and we've talked about this. You win with people and you win with mental and physical toughness. That's what this league is about. So, in order to be physical, in order to play with mental physical toughness, you have to add players to your team that possess those qualities. So, if you say that's what you're about, well, then it's our responsibility to go out there and find it and like nobody epitomizes more than more than Keelan, which is why he's sitting in a chair next to us. Keelan, um you were speaking yesterday about Right here. Jonathan Alexander, Houston Chronicle. Nice to meet you. Uh you were speaking yesterday about uh kind of your mindset. Um other people have described you as kind of like playing with like a nasty mindset. Um like you finish people. But, I'm just curious how you adopted that. Where that came from, what what influences that? Is it Is it your upbringing, where you came from? What influences that? I mean, I think you can point to a lot of a of areas. I think I'm just first and foremost, I'm a competitor. I just love to compete in everything I do and I think if you're a true competitor, you want to finish it like as an offensive lineman, you want to put the dude in the dirt. I mean, you want to play it that way till the whistle. Um you want to compete at a high level um and you want to be the best about it. So, I think that's just, you know, just the competitor in me. I've always had that fire about me. So, I think that's where it comes from. Uh this is for Nick and DeMeco. Obviously, whenever a player gets picked, there's always talk, "Well, this team wanted him before, so you had to go up and get him." How do you prepare for that? Like maybe leading up to it where you talk about acting stuff up and then in the moment and how hectic can it be when you want a guy and you anticipate that maybe team in front of you would want the same guy. Yeah, it's really about organization and preparation and then capitalizing the opportunity when it presents itself. So, I mean, DeMeco and I talk, I would say, I mean, 40 times a day. So, we're talking about players, we're talking about different scenarios. He probably wants me out of his office plenty of the time. But, you're always going through different scenarios. And in our situation, say once we got into like 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, you start to look at, "All right, who are the players that are available? Who are some of the players that we would consider taking?" And you kind of create some buckets. And then as you go through, again, we don't really know what other teams are going to do. Like you try to as best you can make an estimation and look at the the roster, "Hey, there's some players that they might be interested in." It doesn't mean that for sure they're going to be you're going to be interested in the same player. And then we look at it through the lens of in the end, what's the best thing for the Houston Texans? We can't worry about what other teams are doing. They're going to make their decisions. We have to make our decisions independent of what anybody else is doing. So, in terms of how chaotic it it's really not. It's pretty fluid. It's ongoing. And we just kind of react and we're ready to go. And if you do a trade, you make a trade and you pick the player. If you can't consummate the trade, then you prepare for the next opportunity in front of you. So, we're pretty consistent. It'll be no different here tonight when we get started here in a few hours. Kenyon, have you had a chance to I know you haven't been in town long, but have you had a chance to meet any other members of the offense since you landed in Houston? Uh yes, sir. Uh C.J. Stroud uh came by, text me. Will text me. Um and C.J. Stroud came by the hotel. We talked for a long time. Um he's a great human being first and foremost, but obviously, we all know how he how he is out there on the grass and he's he's made of the right stuff. So, he's a he's a great dude, man. Uh just great for him to come up there and take the time to come talk to me. Uh Kenyon, right in here. Uh earlier today, it was said by by Coach Keeton that you met with Cole Popovich before the draft. Um what were those conversations like and what did you think about the overall offensive approach that he was kind of talking with you about? Yeah, I mean, I I really loved my time with Coach Pop. Um he put me through a lot of things that, you know, he's looking for and, you know, in terms of how he's going to throw hands, all them all them details kind of thing and, you know, different than what I did in college, but, you know, I just soaked it in. Just try to take the coaching. Um he's he's there to coach me and uh see what I had, see how I was moving and I I really enjoyed the time and the Zoom I had with him. I'm just talking ball and I loved it. Uh DeMeco, um when you were looking at Kenyon's film and and and you were obviously liking what you were seeing, what what what what did you and and Nick and Kenyon envision for him? Uh for me, when I'm I'm watching the film of all these offensive linemen, right? Studying a lot of different guys and when I put on his tape, I typed in the word swarm. And that's what it that's what I saw on tape. That's the type of player that I saw and the envision is he can he play multiple spots on the interior part of the offensive line. Though he spent a lot of time at right guard. He snapped the ball at Senior Bowl, did a really good job of that. Smart young man, bright young man. We're just happy to work with him. See may the best five guys go out there and help us win some games. He's ready to compete. He's talked about how he loves to compete. That's how he gained his edge and that's what we're all about. I saw that competitor mindset. I saw it jump off of the tape and that made it an easy choice. And for us and for me, we're drafting, you see a guy you want. That's why I love working with Nick. We see a guy we want. We see a guy who fits our building, fits what we're about, fits our culture. Let's go get the guy, add him to our team. Uh this is for DeMeco and Nick. When when y'all um hired Popovich as the offensive um line coach, what what was it that y'all liked about Cole Popovich and is is this is it safe to say that the what we've seen with this offensive line is kind of a significant impact of his with with the with the turnover and everything? Go ahead, Nick. Yeah, me hiring Cole, the one thing in the interviewing process, like Cole is a a brilliant coach. He's a very smart guy and he's not just offensive line driven. Like he's very thoughtful in seeing the entire picture of the offensive line, right? And how it all fits together. He's very thoughtful in making sure, "Hey, which guys do I need? What do they do well?" And he he does a really good job. If you guys ever get a opportunity to see him work in his individuals and how he takes the time to coach the guys up on all the fine, small details that's really important for an offensive lineman. And it's him being detailed, being thorough as a coach and never stuck on what he's always done. He's always trying to help his players, always trying to improve his players. And to me, that's the signs of a really good coach. He's a excellent communicator, does a really great job on game day as well. We need to make adjustments. Cole is the guy who sees it, can make the adjustments and get us in the right right situation. So, he's all the things you want in a coach. Nick and I guess to an extent, DeMeco, how much of what happens on changes what you would maybe expect to do on day two? I know you guys moved back about 20 spots in the third round, but also, you know, now you have Kenyon, offensive lineman. Would you, you know, still be expected to maybe draft an offensive lineman as well? How much changes from after things are done in the first round to the second round? Always open for business on anything. Doesn't necessarily take us just because you select one player doesn't necessarily take you out of either a player or a position. Like we'll go back to what we've kind of done today is look at the board and said, "All right, here are certain players graded to a certain level. What are our opportunities? We're scheduled to pick right now at 38 with five or six picks in. What are options? Who are the players that we've identified? If they're available, we pick them, great. If not, we move back. And then we're scheduled to pick at 59 and then 91 or whatever it is right now. So, we'll just follow the board, look at our grades. In the end, we always go back to our grades. What do we say about the player? What have our scouts said? What have the coaches said? And then just kind of work ourselves around the board and try to make good smart decisions. I mean, we didn't go into the draft last year anticipating we were going to draft draft Jaylon Johnson, but that's the way the board fell. So, we took both players. So, if there's an opportunity to draft another offensive lineman that makes sense, we'll certainly consider it. We're not going to rule it out because you really never know when you're going to need these players and what the overall constitution of the team is going to look like. I mean, we can't sit here today and say, "Well, we know what it's going to look like in September." It could change. So, we're always planning for what's in front of us, but we're going to add good players with the right mentality, with the right mindset. Let the players ultimately sort itself out and then if we got to make some decisions at some point, then we'll make decisions we feel are best for the team. Kenyon, Brent Key today was telling me that there was a conditioning test and guys were, you know, trying to get through it. It was a tough one. You were literally pushing your teammates and yelling. Do you remember that? Was that this year or last year? Just what can you tell me about that? And I have a follow-up. Uh yes, sir. I mean, I definitely remember that, but it was just who I am every day. Uh no different conditioning test. First day, um winter jacket drills, inside run. It's just, "Hey, you competitor. You want all your teammates to be wired the same way you are and uh get after it." So, you're going to push some guys to their limit and you hope that they push you to your limit. Iron sharpens iron. So, you still watch even though after you were done, you were watching the tape and critiquing the practice stuff. He said that you were kind of going back and wondering, you know, was the standard, you know, still going the way you wanted it to with your younger teammates? Yeah, I mean, there's a lot of new new faces in there on the O-line over there at Georgia Tech. So, you want to watch the tape. You know, I'm going into practice. Don't know a lot of the guys. So, a lot of new faces over there. So, I just want to see what they're about, see how they play the game. And obviously, when you go to practice, I'm going to hey, if I see something on tape, I'm going to let them know like, "Hey, I think this, yada yada." So, you just you want them to I would love to be a sponge and you want them to just soak it up. Lastly, uh he called you an underrated athlete and they were saying that you ran in the 4.9s. You were actually disappointed to run like I think it was 5.05 at the at the combine. And you basketball, that stuff. What is your background in those sports and other thing kind of say about you as an athlete? Thank you. Uh yes, sir. I mean, I think I'm a good athlete, obviously. You know, I don't want to toot my own horn, but I think I move well. Um grew up didn't play offensive line till I got to college. So, grew up playing tight end and D-line. Um played all sorts of sports, played basketball, threw shot put. So, you know, jack of all trades kind of deal. Kenyon, I wanted to ask you a little bit more about um what you were saying earlier when C.J. came by. Um did y'all break bread? What did you make of him coming over to the hotel and and and what can you tell us about, I guess, the general message? Yeah, I mean, I think first of all, he was just excited. Um you know, you could tell he's a leader. He's made like I said, he's made of the right stuff. So, he just wanted to come over there and just, hey, congratulate me. Um just, you know, welcome me and uh just, I mean, just talking life, you know? Nothing special. Uh just guys being guys, just talking ball and wishing me luck. And he said, "Hey, if you need anything, I'm here for you." So, what you want your quarterback. Kenyon, you were a player that entered the transfer portal and went to Georgia Tech and you mentioned that you didn't play offensive line till you got to college. Can you talk about your relationship with Brent Key and what he meant to be able to help you get to where you are today. Yeah, I mean Brent Key's a great ball coach, great man, just what he stood for at Georgia Tech. Um the way he ran the program, I think, you know, that's the way it should be ran. It was built on toughness. It was just built on how we were going to be committed, how we were going work with your teammates. It was it was ran the right way and obviously he's a O-line guy, so he's always getting his nose in the offensive line and he and you know, he just developed me in the right way. He'd always bring me in his office, talk life first and foremost and then he'd be like, "Hey, fix this, fix this." So, he he's a really good ball coach and he's, you know, I can credit him for for where I'm sitting today. Pedro Hernandez for Televisa. Keilan, with Houston Texans being so close to Mexico, there's a huge fan base over there in Mexico and Monterrey. Any message to more of our international fans outside of Houston? Heck yeah, I mean, love all my fans. Let's get let's get after it this year. Um let's play some football and uh let's just let's swarm. Let's go let's go win some games. All right. All right, thank you guys. We're going to take a quick Thanks.

title: LIVE: Texans EVP/GM Nick Caserio addresses the media after Day 1 of the NFL Draft
text: Evening. Hope everybody's doing all right. Um round honestly played out the way we sort of anticipated. Think there ended up being I don't know, like seven tackles, two guards, couple quarterbacks, five or six receivers, couple backs, and then and 14 players on defense or whatever it was. Um so um looked at a couple of uh And then, you know, I think moving two spots, it was just more of semantics than more than positioning more than anything else. Um some interest in the player. So, we felt like, all right, we'll just move a couple spots, essentially give up a fifth-round pick, which is essentially what the difference is when you actually do the math. Um you know, to get a player who I think you all just spoke with them, but I would say I mean, the things that stand out about him, I mean, toughness, violence, physicality, playing style, his intelligence. I mean, the basic guy wants to step on your throat in every play. So, which I would say is sort of embodies what our football team is about, the way we play, intense, violent, physical. Like, we're going to run the football this year. Um you know, it was an area that we felt like we wanted to and needed to improve here in the offseason. Hopefully, we've done that. And um I'd say Big Red is hopefully, you know, a part of that. Like, where is he going to play? Like, who the hell knows? I mean, we'll figure out like who the best five guys are. And, you know, put the group out there that we think is going to help us the most. Understanding that we'll probably need eight to 10 guys on the offensive line here at some point. So, um you know, he's a player that again, a good example, transfer up. So, started at obviously a lower level, and transferred over to Georgia Tech. And had a good career there. Um you know, he was at the Senior Bowl. Um you know, we spent a little bit of time with him here um in the spring. I mean, Cole went down there, worked him out. Um so, I mean, he's a player like I think the whole building collectively felt strongly about. So, you know, that sort of worked out the way that we it hoped it would. So, you know, excited to get him here, and we'll be back to the drawing board here tomorrow. Um I think we got 38, uh whatever, 59. Kind of like picking third round just got moved down there a little bit. So, try to take advantage of our opportunities here tomorrow um with those picks. Um I'm sure we'll get some calls, and you know, we'll kind of see what makes sense relative to moving back or sitting and picking. So, just kind of taking it here, you know, one pick at a time, but you know, definitely excited about Keilan and the things that he brings to the table. So, take some questions. I think when you look at Did you have a specific moment in meeting him or or watching him and that that Uh yeah, when you put the tape on. I mean, everybody that watched him, I mean, your notes basically say physical, tough, strong. Good run blocker, good at the point of attack. Um he's probably more athletic than maybe people think he is. Um he's got some technique things that he can certainly clean up, which I think one of the things with the workout, you know, sometimes you're trying the I mean, how do they apply the coaching? Uh I mean, I wasn't a player like the makeup on this guy is like elite. Like couple of the metrics that we have in our and when we grade players, I mean, in like four or five categories, like there were one player there's one player in the draft that our scouts graded the way that they did, and it was him. So, like that was like, okay. It We didn't talk to him at the combine cuz we didn't need to. Like and then we might not even interviewed him at the Senior Bowl cuz we didn't need to. So, I mean, there was a couple touchpoints here and there we felt like, but just put the tape on, watch the guy play. And I'd say like the program that Coach Key runs down there at Georgia Tech, we got a lot of respect for their program. I mean, Coach Key is a former offensive lineman. Um and again, I think like Big Red, like who he is, is emblematic in like what you saw tonight. I mean, the basic guy was in an Airbnb with him and his wife, and that was pretty much it. You know, you see some of these other draft parties, some of you, you know, you got it took like a circus. I mean, this guy's all ball. He's all football, doesn't really care about anything else. Wants to punch people in the mouth. Yep, that works here. So, I mean, that's what you see on tape, which is I'd say part of the intrigue with the player. How valuable is it to you guys that he's comfortable playing all three positions? Yeah, we'll see. I mean, he'll probably play wherever like he needs to play. So, I'd say all three inside guys. Like again, we've talked about this. You got some guys that are center only, some guys that are guard only, some guys that can play all three spots. So, we'll see how it goes. I mean, your ball. So, I mean, where's he going to play? I mean, we'll see. Like, nobody knows. So, we'll figure that out as we go. Go ahead. Got through that car accident, had a pretty pretty bad foot injury. When you see a player like that that's already been through something, what does that tell you about the mental toughness that you hope for? Yeah, I kind of think it kind of speaks to his personality, Aaron. I think that was like the appealing thing about this player. I mean, you alluded to the accident that he went through, but like I said mentioned a little bit earlier, talked about a transfer up. I mean, he didn't start at the biggest program. I mean, nobody's ever heard of the program that he started. And then he went to Georgia Tech, and he made an impact. So, I think that's speaks to who he is as an individual, his mindset, and it really is emblematic of what this program, the foundation, the principles that that we talk about, that Demeco talks about, that I talk about, that the players talk about, that we want to have in our players. Cuz in the end, like you're going to need that on Sundays. So, I mean, it's He's a really He's a great kid. Um cares a lot about football. Um he's overcome some things. Um you know, I think his wife is a big influence in his life. Um I think Coach Key has been a big influence on him. Um like I said, we have a lot of respect for Coach Key and the program that he he runs and and what he's about. They look, [clears throat] they won I don't know, nine or 10 games or whatever it was. And they probably beat some teams that they like nobody thought they should beat, but they have a lot of belief um in themselves. Um and I think Big Red certainly falls in that category. With the offensive line's shortcomings this last season, uh just what's the timeline in getting him in into the lineup? I mean, the best five guys will play. So, like whoever those guys are, I mean, we're not going to put any timelines on anybody. So, whenever they're ready, they're ready. And we'll figure out like who's going to be out there. I mean, it might start one way, and then it might shift. I mean, there's a lot of things that can happen. So, I mean, we don't put any timelines on anybody. I mean, the players ultimately determine what the timeline is. So, when a player is ready, we'll put him out there. Um if that's the best option, then that's the guy that's going to play. James Lightfoot, obviously he's an alum and a football player for Georgia Tech. Did that help at all with the scouting process? I mean, you just got all the schools with uh Was that helpful at all? >> Yeah, I mean, I think other than like them maybe giving more to the alumni fund, I mean, I probably wouldn't do much into it. I mean, uh you know, I mean, James does a good job. I think the scouting group does a phenomenal job. I mean, like the pro staff, the college staff. I mean, essentially like when we were going through the draft, we were looking at each team, okay, what are their needs, what do we think they're going to do? And whoever had that team had an answer in a heartbeat. And honestly, it played out exactly the way I thought. So, I mean, I have a lot of respect and appreciation for our group. They work really, really hard. They take a lot of pride. They care. They're informed. And they understand their teams, and they provide incredible information so that ultimately we can make good decisions for the organization. So, that's the most important thing. On his scouting report, on his scouting report, it talks about how great of a run blocker he is and how he's able to maul the, you know, defensive line in front. But they say that some of his weaknesses is pass blocking. How much can Cole Popovich help him with that? Yeah, I don't know who said that or like what scouting reports we're like what reading or who we're relying on. I mean, all players have areas that they can improve and fix. So, I mean, doesn't matter who they are, what they are. So, again, I don't know what scouting report or who said that. I mean, we don't really care. What we care about is what they do when they walk in our program and what what we're going to ask them to do. All we want to do is see a player like take coaching, improve, and apply what we're teaching. All that's all we care about. And the same bowl, he took a couple snaps at center. Were you able to observe that? What did you think? Uh yeah. I mean, I think sometimes probably hard to extrapolate too much, you know, when a guy just goes down there in the Senior Bowl for 3 days, and you know, has a couple snaps, and like while you're making a projection based off of that. So, um again, we'll see how that goes. I mean, if the guy can put his hand on the ball, then okay, what does that look like? And the communication that's involved with it. So, again, like when a player walks in the building, like we'll put things on his plate, see what they can handle, um and see how quickly they can adapt and adjust to what we're asking them to do. What was I think was was the the you know, interaction with with this kid at the Senior Bowl? Was Was this sort of like the coup de grace on top from what y'all seen on the tape? Or did just Was this sort of like put the period behind this is the way you want him at on your draft board? >> Uh yeah, I mean, I think we grade the player in the fall, and you assign a grade, and there wasn't a lot of variation or deviation like after the season. I think one thing you have to be careful about is, okay, you spent all this time in the fall, and then okay, you start making adjustments or changes based on like Senior Bowl and all that. So, I think our scouts and grades are pretty consistent throughout. Um so, you're just evaluating the player, evaluating the performance. Um honestly, I'd be careful to put too much stock in the senior bowl either way because again, it's a short snapshot, small snapshot. So, but everything is all-encompassing at the end. Tape, senior bowl, combine, pro day, workout, if you do a visit, those zooms, like whatever the case may be. So, you try to accumulate as much information and create a profile on the player as possible. And then just try to take that information and say, "Okay, here's what we think we have in a player." Understanding, you know, there might be some deviation or variation when they get here. So, it's all part of the process, all part of the evaluation. To follow up with Zay's question about Cole Pop, because obviously he met with Cole Pop and he went through a little workout. How much does that interaction help, I guess, the evaluation process for you guys? Yeah, it's a part of it. So, we do that with all of our coaches. Like we had a number of our coaches out in the spring. So, whether it's a private workout, whether they go to the pro day. I mean, every team has the ability to basically zoom with the player three times. So, you have different touch points. And a lot of that is like football. So, yeah, we like we value their opinion. Hey, what do you think? What information are you gathering? Is it different than maybe what we already had or something new? So, like we value our coaches and their opinions and what they think of the player at the various touch points. Again, it's a snapshot. It's not the only like we're going making a decision based off of that. It's an accumulation over time. Um and I'd say with this particular player, it's pretty consistent. What are we getting in return? Yeah, yeah, I know you mentioned you'll let, you know, the position play itself out. Was the fact that he is multiple, was that intriguing for you guys or or do you all envision something more? I'd say just generally speaking, I mean, any player if they have some degree of position flexibility or versatility, I mean, there's value in that. Again, even going back to tackle, some tackles are left tackle only, some are right tackle only, some can potentially swing and do both. So, again, you try to put the player in a position, just see if if they can handle that assignment. You might think theoretically, "Oh yeah, they should be able to do it." Or he did it here, but then they come to find out, you like go down the road, I mean, I'd say just past experience, I've seen it happen both ways. Like, "Oh, you think this guy, he should just be able to project inside." Or he played left tackle, should have no business no problem playing right tackle. And then you put him over there on the right side and it's a disaster. It's like, "Well, let's just keep him over there where he belongs." So, again, try to see what a player can handle and ultimately try to fit him in best where like they're comfortable, we're comfortable. Um and then go from there. Thank you. All right, thanks. I'll send you all the schedule for tomorrow.

title: Fernando Mendoza: ‘Blessed To Be in This Position’ | 2026 NFL Draft
text: for Adam Hill, Las Vegas Review Journal. Um, you you said to Paul you you weren't sure even till tonight. So, did they not tell you along the way in the process like you're the guy to to be ready and you really had to wait till today? And I guess um you know where in the process did you feel like this would be a good fit for you? >> Well, whatever team was going to select me and be a good fit, but deep down my heart, I knew the Raiders are most likely going to be the best fit because of the coaching staff. I think it really fits my play style great because all the great teammates on offense and defense. They're stacked because of the great ownership. Whether it's Mr. Davis, Mr. Brady. I mean, what a better situation to walk into. So, I think all the stars are aligning here and I'm just very blessed to be in this position. >> Hey, Fernando. Uh, congratulations. You mentioned Mr. Brady. I've seen you over the years talk about how much you looked up to him throughout ever since he started playing football. What does it mean for him to be part of the group that uh drafted you and what have your interactions been with him like so far? >> It means a ton and I think it's a huge edge for the football club to be able to have such a a source of knowledge, intelligence, and experience all in one, especially as an owner. It's something very rare that you get. So, I'm looking forward to diving in, getting all the resource I can from him and learning from him, the great coaches, and the other great players we have on the team. Hello, Fernando. This is Hondo Carpenter. When you look back at your career through high school to Cal to IU to the Raiders, it's really been a journey of faith, both your personal faith, but also betting on yourself. You could have gotten more money or gone other places, but you chose IU because of the coaching. I'm just curious, how much is faith in you and not not just your spiritual faith, but your faith in and trust in you and what you do and your team part of who you are as a man? >> Well, first off, I'm a man of God and I believe that God has a plan. He's blessed my family, blessed me, and I just can't thank him enough. And second of all, I also think that f that fortune favors the bold and that sometimes when you're bold and you bet on yourself, it'll work out most of the times. And if it doesn't work out, at least you'll be able to at least sleep easy at night 20 years down the road knowing you did everything possible to accomplish your goals. And that's what I look forward to doing, doing everything possible to accomplishing my goals with this football club and helping any way I can. Fernando, how you doing? Q Myers, Raider Nation Radio 920. Uh, we know that the journey is just now beginning in the NFL. What is it that you're most excited about the opportunity that you bring to this team and just what you want to learn and what you're going to bring when you get boots on the ground? >> Well, I'm really excited to meet everyone at the Silver and Black organization, Raider Nation, and just really excited to learn what a great ownership group we have, what a great coaching staff, and what a great players. I'm blessed. >> So, what have the last uh 24 hours or so been like for you? >> Um been around a lot of people, a lot of celebrating with my friends and family and um a long night and a long travel. >> What do you think of the facility? >> I love it. It's beautiful. Yeah, it's my first time seeing it. So, um yeah, it's nice. >> Have you had a chance to meet any of your new teammates or anyone? I met Ko. He was out on the field. Um, I just spoke to him a little bit. >> What was that conversation like? >> Just basically told him it was honor to meet him and that I'll be learning a lot from him and asking asking him a bunch of questions. >> What did you ask him? >> He didn't ask me anything. >> Oh my god. >> What did you ask? >> Oh, I told him I was going to ask him a ton of questions leading into, you know, meeting room, whatever it was. Um, I'm just going to try to learn as much as I can from him. >> How familiar are you with his with his game? >> Fairly, you know, from his, you know, Chicago days. Um, there's no way you would just play football on social media without seeing a few clips of Killa Max. So, >> what kind of questions are you going to ask him? Like, what what are you most excited to learn from somebody like that? >> Really, he's been in the game so long, right? So, how he's done that, how he takes care of his body really, what's his his routine when it comes to day-to-day things. And then when it when we're in the meeting room, um you know, his pass rush plan, his plan on first and second down, how he approaches different looks on the field, just trying to pick his brain as much as I can. >> Jim and Joe, yesterday mentioned just about your motor and just your relentlessness. Just what where does that come from? And what what about your mentality? mentality allows you to play that way. >> I think it just that's just how was how I've always played the game. Um, growing up it was really I didn't really have a bunch of IQ. I'm 16 years old just playing football. Um, I always had awareness for the game and what always stuck out on the film was my motor and my relentlessness. So, it's not something I think about, it's just something that that happens. >> You uh decided on a number yet? Um, you know, I can't get three, but um, I'll probably just go back to 90, my um, original college number. >> Why? Why? Um, I mean, just does it have any meaning beyond it just being your original college number? >> No, it was just the first number I ever had coming into college. Um, why not go back to it? >> And would you try to get three or no? >> Um, the odds are kind of zero, but um, no. Uh any teammates re reach out to you, Mario, anybody from uh Miami? >> Yeah, Coach Chris, JT called me as soon as I got drafted. Um you know, I still talk to Ruben and Ahmad every day. So um yeah, everybody, you know, just congrat bless you, congratulating me and um yeah, that's about it. >> What did it mean for you and Ruben to both get selected and only seven seven picks apart? It's, you know, what we've been working working like on throughout the past three years. Um, we talk about it all the time. We did talk about it all the time throughout the season. You know, what we could potentially do. Um, but you know, when I see when I saw his face on the TV, um, I really almost shed a tear. I was so happy he got picked up. >> who also forgot to say just now, but to your >> to your chart is 90. >> I think Well, I'm not sure. I thought it they told me it was available. If not, then >> if not, I'll I'll just pick another number. Yeah. >> You mentioned Coach Taylor at Miami. What What did you learn from him working with him? >> Really, the biggest thing about Coach JT is he's a simple coach. He's not going to try to do too much. Like I've watch like you watch his tape. He's a simple guy. He, you know, he creates length. He keeps people away from him and he just has a high motor. Um that was the biggest things that stuck out on tape watching his tape. So and he's the same way as a coach like you can learn. Every coach is going to teach you the basic fundamentals of football. But the difference between JT and other coaches is his experience. 14 years in the league, gold jacket, um picking his brain on again um how to watch film, what to look at when you're watching film. um pass, rush, progression, first and second down versus third down, how to take care of my body. Um formation, everything about football, like the game is what he taught me the most of. >> Going to have a a lot of new experiences here coming days, weeks, months. What are you most excited about doing? >> Competing and earning the respect of my teammates. >> How do you how do you go about doing showing up every day on time, ready to work. Um me, the way what we preach at Miami, you know, my last four years, early is on time. So, I always show up early, take care of my body, do everything I have to do pre-practice, and then once you get on that field or in that weight room, compete your butt off, and you know, people respect guys who compete and work their butt off. So, just do that and earn the respect of my coaches and my teammates. What was that moment like when your phone started vibrating last night to ring? >> My heart dropped. I was just I was excited. I knew it was that time. Picked up the phone. Coach Harbaugh was on the phone, talked to me. Um basically said they they really liked my formal meeting at the combine and yeah, it was just everything else was really a blur. I was just it was yes sirs and thank yous just and then yeah man I'm just ready to be here excited to be here. >> Is there anything about the the whole process since obviously you thought about it for a long time but like is there anything that was surprising to you how quickly you got here? How did this happen? I know it's been a whirlwind like anything you didn't expect? >> No, nothing I didn't expect. You hear a bunch of different stories from people who got picked up. Um, so throughout this whole process going from last game into training preparation to combine to pro day to 30 visits to draft day to coming here. Um, you hear all about it. So nothing came to nothing came to like came to me as a surprise. >> Coach Harbaugh talked yesterday about how you know you love to practice, love to play. Why why do you love football? >> Why do I love football? I just love the game. I don't It's like if I asked you why you love pizza, you just love it. You know, you know, it's the game I've been playing since I was 8 years old. Um the physicality, the violence, the technical, like how technical I am in my game. Um just everything that comes with football on the field and off the field, the relationships you can build. Um football is more than just helmet and pads. It's like it's a lifestyle for me. Were you always a a defensive player on that side of the ball? No, >> I've played I played one I played a little bit of tight end. Um I played a year at I play a little bit of receiver. Um but 90% of my time has always been on defense. >> So you seem very calm and collected. What happens to you when you step on that football team? >> I'm not going to lie, it's just it's not something I think about. It's just the way I've been I've played the game my whole life. It's not a switch that I flip. It's not something that I get on the field and have to convince myself to do. It's it's just the way the game is played to me. Um and it's the way it's always been played. >> Just uh talked about Khalil, but you're also joining a room with Tuli Palotu. How familiar are you with his game, if at all? >> I'm not very familiar, but I'm going watch a ton of film. I love watch sorry I love watching football so I'll familiarize myself really quick. >> He's a guy that like you can move inside and rush over guards Khil stuff so you can pretty much rush from anywhere. >> What do you think you're going to bring in terms of some of the interchangeable pieces up front and having a bunch of guys in the room that you know like you rush from the edge and rush from the interior. What do you think that's going to provide? >> I think I'm adding another really good piece to that D line. Um, of course the versatility that I'm able to rush inside and out, but also the size and violence that I play with where I can set an edge on first and second down, a blunt edge. Um, so I think I'm a well-rounded defensive player, and you know, I'm just excited to go out there and compete with them boys. >> In terms of your moves and your your pass rush bag, your toolbox, was there a moment in your college career where you really started to hone different moves? was more of a process over your entire college career building that >> I've changed it throughout the years. Um like I've used to I used to rely a lot on a chop like a chop dip rip but then I started facing old linemen who who are double punchers that punch pretty high and it's hard to chop a high hand. So I kind of transitioned to using a side scissor and just trying different things out. Um, like I spend a lot of time at the facility alone just trying to learn um my body, my steps, how long it takes for me to get to the fight line, where I'm making a move on the tackle, um, rush angles, sorry, um, width, from how far I am from, wherever I'm rushing. Um, so I've done a ton of different stuff alone where I practice what moves I want to use, but it's my bag has gotten better throughout the years to where I can use a bunch of different moves. Are you the type of guy that's watching a lot of like NFL edges and trying to take what they do and implement it into your game or are you more so like you're saying sort of on the flip yourself trying to figure out what works for you personally? >> No, I take I take I take stuff from everybody. Like Ruben is younger than me. When he came in as a freshman, I was a true senior. Um I took stuff from Ruben. Like if I see it and I see that it works and I like it, I'll put it into my game. the way the way I run a T game or one one of our stunts where the tackle penetrates and the the DN sells speed and loops behind him. I seen one of our D tackles run like penetrate a certain way where he was attacking the tackle rather than the guard and the way he was using his hands and I'm like it worked and I see it worked like I told myself I like that so I stole that and put into my game. So I'm always like I'm stealing everybody else's move and putting into mine and making it mine I guess. What was the interaction like with you and coach Harpal when you showed up to the facility today? >> W very welcoming. Um he had a big smile. I had a big smile. I'm I'm typically always smiling. Um but it was, you know, a heartwarming welcome. >> What uh what should the fans expect from you? What are you going to show? >> What should they expect from >> Yeah. What are they what are they going to see? What would you tell the fans that you're going to bring to the table? >> I'm bringing versatility. I'm bringing a pastor's bag and violence and the ability to set a blunt edge.

title: Rob Brzezinski Talks Minnesota Vikings Drafting DL Caleb Banks in Round One of the 2026 NFL Draft
text: Um, well, you guys got KO. I'm sure you told you all about uh Caleb and how excited we are. Just uh really proud of our staff, our coaches, you know, how hard everybody worked um you know to uh to make the selection we made tonight and we're really happy about it and uh ready to roll. >> Questions. What was um your process for analyzing the medical with Caleb and determining obviously that he was good to go from your perspective? >> Yeah, I mean I think you know we we have the best doctors in the country if not the world and um we have complete confidence in them. Um you know there's nothing you know without risk in any player you you select but we feel very good you know about where Caleb will be when it's time to uh go to training camp and um so we're comfortable with the injury. kind of negotiate or balance that understanding that he has a high potential if the injuries aren't a you know a derailer. Yeah, I mean it's it's uh it's it's it took a lot of discussion, you know. I mean, I think none of this you can just look at in a vacuum. So, as we're analyzing Caleb and we're stacking our board, we just stack the board based on the way we see the talent and you're you're analyzing everything and including everything. And um we just felt really comfortable where he was on our board and and the board fell and he was the best player on the board and we took him and uh it was pretty easy. >> Rob, how important did you feel like just with where the roster was, the defensive [clears throat] tackle position was one you guys needed to look at throughout the course of the draft? You know, I mean, just number one, it might not be fair to Flo and his staff, but he's so good at whoever is in that room, making the players play to their potential and uh and put a really good product on the field. Um, none at all really. I mean, we we we wanted, you know, in the ideal world, we needed help there and it worked out that way. Um, so didn't feel pressure at all. There's other players in the draft that we liked on the defensive line and um just really really fortunate for us to get who we thought, you know, was the very very best player, you know, on the defensive line in the draft. >> Rob, with him having the wingspan that he does and just the the reach on the line, how [clears throat] much of a difference does that make getting someone like that in that room? >> I mean, I think KO probably talked about it. His his traits are off the charts. You know, you just don't you don't find guys like this. Uh he's got all the ability in the world. Like I I told him I don't even think he realizes how good he can be. And with our coaching staff and the work that he's gonna be put in, I think the sky's is the limit, you know, and um but in this business, it's day by day. He's got to get healthy. He's got to go to camp. He's got to earn a job. He's got all the potential. Um and I think together with his commitment and the resources and the coaching we have, it's going to give him the best chance to be successful. What was it like to get on the phone with him and just share the news with him and his family? >> It was exciting. You know, it was exciting. My my favorite part of the day, though, was uh I I called an old friend and mentor and legend, Scott Studwell, and uh he was kind enough to meet me for breakfast this morning. And uh that kind of got my mind, you know, in the right spot, you know, and I think in today's world, there's so many inputs, you know, and there's AI and there's all these things. and I just sat down with Stud and we had some coffee and and breakfast and we talked about the way it was in the old days and and we're not trying to over complicate this and so a shout out to uh to Stud. We love your brother and uh thanks for your counsel. >> What made you reach out to him? Assuming you reached out to him, what made you do that? >> I respect him so much. I mean I I was going to go through this process for the first time in my career. I've been in a lot of draft rooms with with Stud and he's he's he's amazing at this and uh just really really respect him and his opinion and and uh it was just more of a general conversation but it was very you know I felt like it really grounded me and and I was able to pass that on to our our coaches and and our personnel staff as well. How did you look at it in terms of obviously you talked about Caleb's traits and then the injuries and so how do you look at that and project like where the right place to take him is or where what what the floor of what you can take him. I mean, there's all different ideas. >> You you you stack you stack the players based on ability, um how we like them and and then you got to take into account things like injury, um off-field character, uh you know, all these other things that come into play. And it's it's it's again, it's nothing none of this happens in a vacuum. We stack the board and we keep talking about it and we're weighing all these things and we we manipulate it around until we're comfortable um with the way we have them stacked the impact that they can have on our team and uh then we just follow the board. >> But do you do you think at all about like would he be there on day two or would he be there you know on our next pick or think like was it your analysis that he was >> he might have been there you he might not. You just you just don't know. I just know, you know, on our board, he was the best player there when we selected him and uh we feel outstanding about, you know, the selection. Um if it wasn't for the foot, we would have no chance of seeing them where we picked them, you know, and so we're looking at it as an opportunity from that standpoint to acquire a really unique talent and um we're we're so fired up. >> Was there I mean, you sat in as many drafts as you have. Was there something about the way Stud went about it that stood out to you? >> I mean, Stu was just the most humble uh celebrity superstar or or whatever. And uh you know, Stud just had such a special way about leading people, about creating conversation, collaboration, bringing people together, uh valuing other people's opinion, not thinking like, you know, with his resume and all the things he's accomplished in his scouting history that that he was any better at this than anybody else. Um, you know, and and he had core fundamentals and and and team building philosophies that that he believed in, you know, and and and I respect him and love him as a friend and I don't know what else to say about my guy stud. >> Rob, you you mentioned off-field character. What have you gathered about Caleb's off-field character? >> Uh, excellent. I mean, we're we're really excited about, you know, I mean, everybody has some areas probably to grow in their lives, you know. um all of us do. Um but we're we think he's a tremendous human being. He's a really really good person. He's fun to be around. Uh he loves football. Um I like I said before, I think the interesting thing about him is he doesn't realize how good of a player he can be. Um and it's going to be fun to see Flo and coach Nielsen and the rest of our staff work with him and uh help him reach that potential. Was there any consideration at all or any phone calls moving around the board a trade or was it just not as much of a >> Yeah, I mean there was you know typically you're you're making like we we made all the pre-draft phone calls. We had several conversations during the draft. Um you know nothing materialized for us that we felt like you know made sense and um you know that's part of the process and ultimately you know we wanted to take Caleb where we did and and we're we're thrilled about it. Great. Thanks everybody. >> Go T-Wolves.

title: Rapid Reactions to the Minnesota Vikings Drafting Florida Defensive Lineman Caleb Banks
text: Hey, Caleb Banks. Welcome to Minnesota. I'm your announcer, Paul Allen. I call the games on radio. That's former linebacker Ben Leber back there. We are so excited to see you wear purple. Holy cow, 6-6, 320 and change. Man, the Minnesota Vikings drafted a game changer in Caleb Banks to join an already good defense, one of the better defenses in the NFL last year. So, excellent excellent pick. Best of luck to you, Caleb Banks. Can't wait to meet you. Thing to keep in mind with this pick is that had Caleb Banks not had the foot injury he's going off his 2024 tape. He would have been one of the top five picks in the draft. This kid has potential to be an All-Pro year after year after year to dominate the inside of offensive lines for years to come. And under Brian Flores and that's the other part of it that just blows my mind is versatility. Caleb Banks is such a great athlete. In high school he played he played tight end, he played quarterback, he played wide receiver before just outgrowing all those positions and then moving to defensive line. The versatility is there, the athleticism is there, the size is definitely there. It's just one question. And you get that figured out, Caleb Banks could be one of the biggest selections that the Vikings have made in a very very long time. I'm so excited to see this kid on the turf come this summer. We say it all the time, you build the team in the trenches, offensive line and defensive line. So, here we were thinking this whole time that we had to fill the safety position. But then a guy like Caleb Banks, who we just heard head coach Kevin O'Connell talk about how if he was not injured last year, this is a top 10 talent and a top 10 selection in this draft. So, we got tremendous value at 18. We got a game wrecker at 18 as long as he stays healthy. So, I love the fact that we're building this team once again through the trenches. NFC North offensive lines, you're on the lookout.

title: Chris Johnson meets with the media | Miami Dolphins
text: Tell me about the thrill of being selected by the Dolphins. Did it surprise you and and tell me about the the phone call and your meetings with them prior to the draft? Yeah, man. Definitely surprised me, man. I you know, just sitting there watching the draft obviously seeing different things go down. And you know, I finally saw my phone go off. And I answered and you know, my my service was a little spotty so I couldn't really hear too well. I had to start moving around the house, but once I was able to talk talk with everybody, man, it was just a great feeling, man. Just understanding, you know, a team a team values me enough to to be able to trade up and grab me, man. And like you said, pre-draft meetings went went great with them and I definitely connected with with them and their staff. And man, I'm just excited to get out there and play some ball, man. Isaiah? What's going on, Chris? Isaiah Smalls from the Miami Herald. Welcome to Miami. How you feeling? I'm I'm feeling great, man. Super excited to be out there, man. That's what's up. That's what's up. Uh Sullvan spoke highly of your character and your approach to the game, even going as far as saying that you play with an edge. If you can kind of describe what that edge means to to you and why is it that you play with that? Yeah, for sure, man. I feel like my edge is I could just describe it as being being non-stop relentless, man. And I feel like that that just goes with the culture that I built here being at San Diego State the last 4 years. That's what we preached, man. That we weren't always the most talented defense on the field, but regardless, you know, effort going out outlasts skill every time. So, just going out there with the approach that I'm going to give 100% on the field whether, you know, whether I got the car or don't. Like regardless of what I'm doing, I'm going to be at 100% always. That's what's up. That's what's up. And second one for you. I'm sure you know Half was a secondary coach. Like that's how he got his start on defense. You being his first pick in the secondary certainly means something. From the conversation that you remember, what did he say he liked about your game? Um Uh probably just said that that he feel like I'm a polished player, man. Like I I excel in different areas and I feel like you know, just taking this next jump and being able to work with him and work under him is just going to help me be be the best player I could be and just keep keep on improving. Well, appreciate you, man. Yes, sir. Marcel? How's it going, Chris? Marcel Louis-Jacques with ESPN. Congratulations, man. Welcome to Miami. I guess trading one paradise for the other, right? Going San Diego. That's crazy. But uh you said something that was I think was really interesting just now. For your 4 years at San Diego State and that is a rarity in college football. Now, what was it about your situation that made you say, "I'm staying where I'm put. I'm staying where I signed for all 4 years. I'm not transferring." Yeah, I feel like you know, after I got my start my my junior year and I played that season, you know, a couple teams started calling for me to to you know, obviously hit the portal and go there, but I feel like at the end of the day, my dream was to get to where I am right now, man. I felt like I didn't want to go somewhere and put uncertainties in the air whereas, you know, I get a bag of money, but it's also like who am I going to be competing against? Who am I going to be playing with? You know, what scheme are they going to be running? And I'm like, you know what? I know what I'm going to do here at State. And you know, my dad always always preached to me, man, that you know, if you're talented enough, they're going to come find you, man. So, you know, I put I put my head down and just worked, man, and stayed there. And I feel like, you know, I I have no regrets, man. Exactly what me and my dad preached, man. I feel like it came to life for sure. Appreciate that, man. Nice to meet you and congrats once again. >> Yes, sir. I appreciate it. David? Chris, congratulations and welcome to to Miami. Welcome to the to the Dolphins, man. Yes, sir. The So, the combine you had was was sensational. How do you think the athleticism you showed at that event that translates onto the field? How do you use that athleticism on on the football field? Yeah, for sure, man. Just being able to go out there and show it not only on tape, but also, you know, get the concrete numbers down. I feel like definitely helped me. As far as using that on the field, it just helps me you know, play the game I like to play like like being ultra physical and ultra patient, man. Obviously having some speed, I could be more patient I'm rushing. I don't have to panic as much as, you know, some other guys may. But God blessed me with this talent I have and you know, I just turn around and thank him by using it on the field. And if I could follow up, I know what when we spoke to Jeff Hafley and he mentioned how he evaluates corners. He he he views it as three levels. His first, can they win at the line of scrimmage? Then can they win on in the intermediate routes? And then can they win down the field? How do you view yourself as far as covering those three aspects? Yeah, really all three, man. I feel like obviously I can improve all three as well, but I feel like I'm sound in all three and obviously just understanding, you know, if you lose phase one and two, you know, phase three is where the money happens, man. Where the ball comes. So, being able to to you know, recover and be able to make a play, you know, whenever or wherever you at in relation to the receiver, man. I feel like that's the most important one, but uh definitely just excited to to keep working on my craft and keep improving.
